{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

Alignment Faking Depends on the Value, Not Just the Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03650
arXiv:2611.03650v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Language models can follow a directive when they believe they are monitored and abandon it when they believe they are not, a pattern termed Alignment Faking. Prior work establishes this for harmful-content objectives and a handful of moral-foundations values, leaving open how it distributes across a wider value space. We argue it is value-dependent: whether compliance survives a change in perceived oversight is a property of the model--value pairing, not of the model alone. Our framework profiles Alignment Faking per value, scoring each model-value pair under three conditions: bare (no system prompt), unmonitored, and monitored. On 32 ValueBench dimensions across ten open- and closed-weight models (8B-~675B), compliance gaps span 0.05-0.50, with a distilled 70B above a ~675B model. We observe that majority of the structural variance depends on which model was asked about which value and not on the model or value alone. A six-category taxonomy over reasoning traces tracks the behavioural shift: training-signal reasoning dominates under monitoring and value-conflict reasoning dominates when unmonitored. We package per-model results as value cards, extending model cards with behavioral disposition. Code and data are available at https://github.com/respailab/VALET.

Abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects large language model agents to external tools and services through official SDKs that implement message validation and session logic. We present MCPGuard, an automated LLM-based framework for detecting specification-to-SDK conformance gaps. Its structural track aligns JSON Schema constraints with normalized SDK models and produces constraint-specific evidence. Its behavioral track extracts normative prose rules, retrieves bounded function-level slices, and audits them with LLMs for candidate omissions. Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03684
arXiv:2611.03684v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Language models serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as ``The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is'', a small general-purpose model may answer ``the alkyne group'' instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether ($\mathrm{R{-}S{-}R'}$) to thiol ($\mathrm{R{-}SH}$), added to ether ($\mathrm{R{-}O{-}R'}$), lands nearest alcohol ($\mathrm{R{-}OH}$). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5\% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning reorganizes it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

Abstract: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) aims to enable AI systems to autonomously build and improve AI systems themselves, including models, harnesses, and underlying infrastructure. However, existing studies on automated model training primarily focused on workflow- or harness-level optimizations, rather than internalizing the ability to conduct post-training into the model itself. results:
The search turned up no Georgia data center ballot measures. Ohio had most of the 2026 local measures, and early returns from the November 3 vote mostly favored limits. Most of these results are preliminary, and the sources below are secondary reports of Ballotpedia's data.

- **Georgia:** Ballotpedia's list of data center ballot measures includes none in Georgia.
- **Ohio count:** Ohio accounts for 20 measures across 17 jurisdictions, more than half of the total. Those numbers changed as the list was updated. A later count put Ohio at 21 of 41 measures nationally on the November 3 ballot.
- **Early returns:** One analysis of Ballotpedia's posted returns found that early returns lean toward limits in 30 of the 35 local data center measures with vote counts. The five that lean toward development are all in Ohio.
- **Specific Ohio results:** In Granville, the ban was trailing, with 18% Yes and 82% No. In Ashville, Ballotpedia has marked a measure as defeated. Local coverage reported that in each of central Ohio's five races, communities voted to reject data centers.
- **Earlier 2026 votes:** Per Ballotpedia, in the six such measures voters had already decided, the side favoring limits won each time.

Caveats: the results come from secondary sites and news outlets, not Ballotpedia directly. Counts vary across sources, and several measures had no votes posted yet at the time of the search. Check Ballotpedia's data center measures page and official county board results for final outcomes.

# WorkOS says attacker used ARTEX AI to breach internal sales app

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 3, 2026

- 0



Developer platform WorkOS suffered a data breach after a threat actor accessed business contact records and summaries of customer communications.



According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.



Based on evidence from the investigation, no WorkOS app data or production services were accessed or affected.



WorkOS is a developer infrastructure company that provides APIs, SDKs, and tools for integrating services such as enterprise authentication, single sign-on (SSO), user management, and identity management into applications.



According to its website, at least 3,000 companies use its services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Perplexity, Snowflake, Plaid, Webglow, and Netlify.



“On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team,” the company says in an incident alert .



Data accessed by the attacker includes:





- Business contact details (names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from the CRM systems)


- Customer account histories (product usage and connection or directory health)


- Customer communications (summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations)


- Business account and relationship information (account histories, information about sales and customer relationship)



After detecting the intrusion, WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application and reviewed its access controls on internal tools.



The company also contracted an independent forensics and incident response firm to track the unauthorized activity and determine its full impact.



The company promised to notify affected customers directly, and warned its users to remain vigilant for phishing or social engineering attempts leveraging the exposed information.




# ARTEX AI likely powering the attack


WorkOS’s announcement says the attack used an AI-powered offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.



Company founder Michael Grinich shared more details , saying that the attacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite that has been observed in multiple incidents this year.



Released earlier this year by Chinese developers, the platform was available as an open-source project for offensive security.



ARTEX AI became private after it was used in attacks targeting South Korean banks , but several forks of its code are still available.



More recently, CrowdStrike revealed that cyber-espionage group “Vapor Panda” used the pentesting framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organizations.



Previously, the non-profit cybersecurity organization DIVD also revealed that the same framework powered the attacks it suffered last September .



Grinich explained that the investigating team identified user agents such as ‘artex-enrich/1.0’ and ‘norma/0.4’ in web requests from the threat actor.



The founder assured that the cybersecurity incident has now been fully contained and promised to share more information about the attack after the investigation completes.

# UK school estate hit by 3AM ransomware in suspected AI-assisted attack

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 3, 2026

- 09:00 AM

- 0



A 3AM ransomware affiliate targeted a school estate in the UK and successfully encrypted around 37 of nearly 50 machines reached from an unmanaged host.



Researchers at cybersecurity company Bitdefender believe the threat actor may have used AI-generated commands and an automated agentic loop to carry out the operation.



The conclusion is based on a sequence of repeated commands that were slightly modified at each attempt and issued at roughly regular intervals of 40 to 100 seconds.



"We were not able to access the machine the attacker worked from, so we cannot document anything about the language model itself: which model it was, whether it ran locally or remotely, or even whether a person was copying and pasting instructions and results between the implant and the model," Bitdefender explains .



The researchers note that they could only document the behavior, and it looked similar to an agentic loop.





Attack overview

Source: Bitdefender





The malicious activity spanned between September 10 and19, but Bitdefender could not establish the attacker’s initial access method.



The threat actor used a modified public PowerShell tool to extract and decrypt credentials stored on three Veeam backup servers, copied a Chrome database containing credentials, and deployed Mimikatz and LSASS memory-dumping tools.



They mapped domain relationships and searched logon-script folders for references to other schools, eventually creating two backdoor domain administrator accounts named ‘library’ and ‘svc_bkpmon.’



After stealing financial data from compromised machines, the attacker configured two-way trusts between three previously separate Active Directory domains to expand their reach.



In the final stage of the attack, they attempted to remove Sophos and Bitdefender protection from reachable hosts, delete system-state backups, and deploy 3AM’s Rust-based encryptor. They succeeded in about 37 cases.





Attack timeline

Source: Bitdefender





The 3AM ransomware threat emerged in 2023 and came to public attention when an attacker deployed its Rust-based ransomware after LockBit was blocked.



Researchers later linked the operation to the Conti and Royal ransomware gangs, and affiliates have been observed using email bombing and spoofed IT support calls to access corporate networks.



A notable past victim is Kootenai Health, where an August 2024 attack exposed personal information belonging to more than 464,000 patients .



Regardless of the current level of AI tool involvement in 3AM attacks, Bitdefender’s observations suggest the threat actors appear to be experimenting with them heavily.



Earlier today, the NCSC in the UK published this year’s ‘The State of the Cyber Nation’ report, urging critical infrastructure to prepare for AI-powered ransomware attacks by 2028.

# Voters in ten states will vote on data center-related ballot measures November 3

By

Mina Vogel

November 3, 2026 at 8:27 PM

On Nov. 3, voters in 10 states will vote on 41 ballot measures affecting local data center policy.

A “yes” vote on 28 of these measures would limit data center development through policies such as bans or moratoriums. A “yes” vote on the remaining 13 measures would facilitate data center development through policies like zoning.

Voters have already decided six measures this year and, in each case, a majority of voters favored greater limits on data center development, either by approving new restrictions or requirements or by rejecting a measure that would have facilitated or supported development. Including these measures, and three that voters will decide after Nov. 3, Ballotpedia is covering 50 local ballot measures in 13 states related to data centers this year.

Ohio voters will decide on 21 measures, more than any other state. Illinois follows with seven measures. Maine voters will decide four, and Kansas voters will decide three. Voters in California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, and Wisconsin will decide one each.

State policies on data centers

State and local governments can affect data center construction through policy actions like permitting, zoning, and tax incentives. As of April 2026, 38 states had created tax incentives to encourage data center construction.

State and local governments can also use some of these policy actions to prevent or limit data center construction, for example through moratoriums (temporary halts) on issuing permits for new projects. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) issued an executive order for the first state-level moratorium on data center construction. This one-year moratorium barred state regulators from issuing permits for new data centers expected to use 50 megawatts or more of electricity. Other states have also issued moratoriums on administrative measures like tax breaks and environmental permits for data center construction.

What the Nov. 3 ballot measures would do

Twenty-eight measures, if approved, would limit data center development:

- Seventeen would ban data centers. Twelve of these would ban data centers above a certain size threshold. For example, one measure in Kansas would ban data centers using more than 25 megawatts of electricity. Five would ban all data centers.

- Three would issue six-month moratoriums on data center development. One measure for a moratorium in Wells, Maine, would also retroactively "nullify any final permit, license, or other approval of a new or expanded Data Center issued by a municipal reviewing authority within 45 days of the effective date."

- Two measures in Ohio would establish zoning regulations for unincorporated areas of the local jurisdictions. If the measures are successful and the areas are covered by zoning regulations, they would have to be zoned for a use consistent with data center construction (such as industrial) for a project to be built there.

- One measure in Ohio would require voter approval for data center projects above land, water, and power use thresholds, while another measure in Wisconsin would require voter approval for a specific data center project if it costs more than $450 million.

- A measure in North Dakota would require independent professional review and a public hearing for projects exceeding various land area, power, and water use thresholds, as well as projects requiring a major air quality permit.

- A measure in Ohio would require data center developers receiving tax incentives to provide financial guarantees to the community.

- Two non-binding measures in Illinois would express voter disapproval of data center projects.

Thirteen measures, if approved, would facilitate data center development:

- One measure in Nevada would add data centers as an approved use for a particular area of land.

- One measure in Ohio would uphold a town agreement with a specific data center company.

- Four measures in Wilmington, Ohio would rezone specific areas of land from residential to industrial uses, allowing data center construction at these sites. According to WCPO News , a specific data center company may build on this land if it is rezoned.

- Seven non-binding measures in Illinois, New Jersey, and Ohio would express voter approval of data center projects.

Voters in four states have already voted on six data center-related measures.

- On March 10, voters in Canterbury, New Hampshire, approved a ban on data centers 83.6% to 16.4%.

- On April 7, voters in Port Washington, Wisconsin, approved an initiative 66.4% to 33.6% requiring voter approval for the city to create a Tax Incremental District if projects in the district cost $10 million or more.

- On June 2, voters in Monterey Park, California, approved a ban 88.3% to 11.7%.

- On Aug. 4, voters in Augusta Township, Michigan, defeated a measure 89.6% to 10.4% that would have rezoned specific areas of land for a proposed data center.

- On Aug. 11, voters in the village of Wrightstown, Wisconsin, defeated a nonbinding measure 87.3% to 12.8% that would have recommended village actions to support data centers.

- On Sept. 8, voters in Nottingham, New Hampshire, approved a one-year moratorium on data center permitting 90.3% to 9.7%.

On Dec. 1, voters in Clarksville, Arkansas will decide whether to uphold two different city bond issue ordinances intended to support a data center project. On Dec. 15, voters in Mandan, North Dakota will vote whether to ban data centers using 25 megawatts or more.

Click here to learn more about data center-related ballot measures in 2026.

COLUMBUS, Ohio (WCMH ) — Ohio is home to more data center ballot issues than anywhere else in the country, and five are in central Ohio.

According to Ballotpedia, 41 data center ballot issues are up for consideration in the U.S. on Election Day. By far, most are in Ohio, at 21. In each of central Ohio’s five races, communities voted to reject data centers.

Ohio is home to nearly 200 data center projects. Data centers have been in the state since at least 2012 but have received significant public attention in the past year. Ohioans living near data centers or proposed data centers often take issue with light, air and noise pollution, and land and utility use.

# Grove City: Referendum requirement

According to preliminary results, Grove City’s Issue 28 is expected to pass with 100% of the unofficial vote counted. The citizen-led charter amendment will require a referendum – or citizen vote – on any large-scale developments that would take up 50 or more acres, use more than 20 megawatts at peak capacity or consume more than 500,000 gallons of water per day.

# Pataskala: Prohibits construction

With 100% of the unofficial vote counted, Pataskala is expected to update its charter to ban large data centers that have a monthly demand of 25 megawatts or more. The issue was put forth by citizen organizers concerned by the impact of possible data center projects.

# Sunbury: Prohibit construction

With 100% of the unofficial vote counted, Sunbury residents appear to have passed a measure to update their charter and ban data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of energy or more a month. Residents are particularly concerned by a possible hyperscale Amazon project , although the project’s fate remains unclear despite the measure’s passage.

# Ashville: EdgeConneX referendum overturned

With 100% of the unofficial vote counted, Ashville is projected to overturn an agreement between the village and data center EdgeConneX guiding negotiations over two data centers. Overturning the agreement may shift what benefits EdgeConneX and the village receive from the projects, but will not stop construction, which is already underway.

# Granville: Prohibits construction

With 100% of the unofficial vote counted, Granville village residents are expected to update their charter to ban the construction of any data centers with peak loads of more than 25 megawatts. Unlike many issues, Granville residents were acting on general preventative measures rather than a specific data center proposal.

results:
Democrats appear to have won both Public Service Commission seats up in the November 3, 2026 election, according to the search results. I found no official certified results, so treat this as preliminary.

- **Winners:** Capital B News reports that Democrats gained control of the Public Service Commission for the first time in more than 20 years, naming Peter Hubbard and Sheila Edwards as winners. Heatmap similarly says both Hubbard and Edwards won, securing a 3–2 Democratic majority.
- **Data centers:** The PSC approved about 9,985 MW of new generation in December 2025, and approximately 80 percent of which is expected to power data centers. Under the agreement, Georgia Power agreed to cover the costs through 2031 if data center demand doesn't show up as expected. Critics and candidates still debate whether these protections are strong enough. Whether those protections are strong enough is the central debate in this election.
- **Rates:** The commission ordered a freeze of Georgia Power base rates through 2028. Hubbard's office says he helped pressure Georgia Power to lower rates by $4 per month. Heatmap reports that rates in Georgia have gone up by less than 1% across the state on average over the past year, but more than 18% over three years.

Sources conflict on some details. Capital B News says the election was won by Democrats for the first time in over 20 years, while Heatmap notes that Democrats had already taken two seats in the 2025 special election. Both agree on the 3–2 Democratic majority outcome, though only Heatmap states the majority explicitly.

results:
The search didn't turn up the Newsweek article or the 89.6% figure, so I can't confirm that number. The results do confirm the core outcome: Augusta Township voters rejected the rezoning in the August 2026 primary.

- **The result:** WEMU reported that voters in Augusta Township have overwhelmingly overturned a rezoning that would have allowed the construction of a large data center. Another WEMU item says the results were rather emphatic.
- **The vote:** The ballot question was set for the Aug. 4 primary, and would give township residents a chance to overturn the rezoning needed for the project, from agricultural residential to general industrial.
- **The background:** The board approved the change in July 2025. The Augusta Township board voted unanimously in favor of conditionally rezoning 522 acres for a data center proposed by New York City-based developer Thor Equities. Residents then gathered signatures to force the referendum. One petition drive reported 957 petition signatures, above its goal of 700.
- **Recall effort:** Separately, township residents are gathering signatures to put forth a recall of all members of the township board in November on the basis of their data center rezoning vote.

The results don't say what share of the vote the rezoning lost, so the 89.6% figure needs checking against the Newsweek piece or the township's official canvass.

########## Knowingly Wrong
cs.CL.txt-arXiv:2611.05287v1 Announce Type: new
cs.CL.txt-Abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.
########## Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors
cs.CL.txt-arXiv:2611.05358v1 Announce Type: new
cs.CL.txt-Abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.
########## Can Benign Skills Induce
cs.CR.txt-arXiv:2611.04299v1 Announce Type: new
cs.CR.txt-Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reusable skills to plan tasks, invoke tools, recover from errors, and complete workflows without modifying model parameters. Although these skills are typically developed to enhance benign tasks, they may also make an agent more capable of executing procedures for harmful purposes. We study this risk, which we call skill-induced behavioral misalignment: adding benign skills may cause an agent to execute external actions that violate safety requirements.
########## Voluntary Servitude
cs.CL.txt-arXiv:2611.04393v1 Announce Type: cross
cs.CL.txt-Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.
cs.CR.txt-arXiv:2611.04393v1 Announce Type: new
########## Inter-Agent Influence
cs.AI.txt-arXiv:2611.04556v1 Announce Type: new
cs.AI.txt-Abstract: The deployment of AI agents in multi-agent settings enables inter-agent influence, whereby agents can strategically steer each other's behaviour towards an intended outcome. Such capabilities pose novel risks, as malicious agents could direct others towards harmful actions. In this work we investigate three such capabilities - persuasion, deception, and coercion - across five realistic evaluation environments and a variety of agents instantiated with frontier language models. We observed significant inter-agent influence capabilities; in oversight environments, all tested models shifted overseer decisions from rejection to approval through persuasion, deception, or coercion. We also observed successful influence in non-hierarchical 'peer-to-peer' settings through redirection of a peer's safety research trajectory. As multi-agent deployments become increasingly commonplace, these results point to a pressing need for work on mitigating the risks from inter-agent influence. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Cooperative-AI-Foundation/inter-agent-influence.
########## We Ran a Research Sprint
cs.AI.txt-arXiv:2611.03946v1 Announce Type: new
cs.AI.txt-Abstract: Generative AI tools for research are widely deployed, yet individual productivity gains do not guarantee better team research. We argue that how AI use is structured matters alongside access. Personal AI tools may amplify two failures under deadline pressure: a consumption bottleneck, in which generation outpaces team-visible evaluation, and AI-induced research silos, in which private human-AI loops displace shared decision-making. We motivate this position with a mechanism-generating pilot: a 100-minute research sprint with twelve researchers in three independently operating teams, within a seventeen-person session. Both patterns recurred across teams and evidence sources. Of 33 logged AI interactions, one was accepted outright and 27 lacked a recorded disposition; missing records alone do not establish absent evaluation. A parallel autonomous pipeline produced a complete draft without in-session human evaluation, illustrating production capacity rather than comparative quality. We propose Human-AI-Human collaboration: an interaction topology in which AI connects researchers' contexts and supports inspectable collective evaluation and decision-making. The pilot does not isolate AI-specific effects from time pressure or workflow practices. We close with seven modular, falsifiable design hypotheses, prioritizing shared context and team-visible evaluation checkpoints for controlled follow-up.

Voters across the country reject data centers • Stateline

News Story

In local elections across the country, Americans voted overwhelmingly to restrict the buildout of data centers in their communities.

Late Tuesday evening, 33 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot . Roughly a dozen similar measures were on the ballot in communities where vote totals had not yet been announced.

The measures included outright prohibitions, temporary moratoriums, limitations on energy use, mandating voter approval before construction and advisory measures urging local officials to restrict data centers.

Only one measure, in North Dakota, resulted in a victory for voters who supported the construction of data centers.

The national backlash to data centers has become a major political issue. Residents in Republican and Democratic cities alike have pushed back on tech companies’ plans to aggressively build data centers to power their artificial intelligence platforms. Local and national activists have raised concerns about energy costs, pollution, water use, noise and conversion of farmland and other open spaces.

According to an NBC exit poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers played a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress.

In some communities, including 21 municipalities in Ohio, residents turned to local ballot measures or referendums in an effort to block the construction of proposed data centers. In nearly every result so far, voters overwhelmingly backed new restrictions or declined to approve measures that affirmed the buildout of such facilities.

Conserve Ohio, a campaign seeking to block data center development, worked with leaders in many of those communities to help draft ballot language.

“It’s one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen, people coming together across communities, putting partisan differences aside and uniting (to oppose data centers),” Nick Owens, an attorney with the group, told Stateline last month.

A poll published by UMass Amherst earlier this year found that only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an AI data center in their community.

By Sasha Rogelberg

Ohio voters rejected the AI buildout almost everywhere it was on the ballot Tuesday, with at least 14 municipalities passing bans or other restrictions on data centers. The Buckeye State is on its way to becoming the prototype for how American voters respond in the face of mass AI infrastructure expansion.
Recommended Video

Ohio residents across 18 municipalities voted on 21 ballot measures on data centers on Tuesday—more than half of the 41 data center-related ballot measures across the country.

With more than 200 operational data centers , Ohio ranks No. 5 among U.S. states in number of data center projects. According to state data, companies plan to invest up to $40 billion in AI infrastructure in the state by 2030.

Plans for AI infrastructure expansion across the country face strong national opposition—including in the form of 125 local data center moratoriums already in place in Ohio. Ohio voters’ decisive stance against the buildout could foreshadow not just future election results, but how stakeholders in the private sector and government respond.

“With over 100 Ohio townships adopting moratoria or restrictions, strong voter turnout against expansion would signal to statehouses nationwide that ratepayer protections, transparency, and grid safeguards should dominate policy agendas,” Keith Durkin, a sociology professor and director of the Ohio Northern University Institute for Civics and Public Policy (ICAPP), told Fortune .

# How did Ohio vote?

In central Ohio, all five communities with data center measures on the ballot voted against data centers. In Sunbury, residents appear to have passed a charter amendment banning data centers that use 25 megawatts or more, with 100% of the unofficial vote counted. The measure was aimed at a possible hyperscale Amazon project, though the project’s fate remains unclear, NBC4 reported. Pataskala voters also approved a charter ban on large data centers.

In Trenton, a ban passed 80% to 20% . Organizers hope it will keep an 18-building Amazon Web Services data center out of the city, though it likely won’t affect a four-building AWS campus already under construction nearby, the Journal-News reported.

In Perry, more than 87% of voters approved a measure requiring developers seeking tax breaks to offer the village financial guarantees. In Wilmington, around 80% of voters rejected rezoning across four separate referendums meant to accommodate a data center project. Results in Oregon weren’t yet available as of midnight.

Ashville residents voted in favor of entirely blocking a data center campus that is already under construction.

The bulk of the ballot measures came from 13 municipalities voting on measures to ban or heavily restrict data centers, including “high impact” campuses using more than 25 megawatts of power. Those measures were on the ballot in the municipalities of Conneaut, Defiance, Granville, Grove City, Hubbard, Monroeville, Oregon, Pataskala, Piqua, Sunbury, Trenton, Upper Sandusky, and Urbana.

Two measures in Monroe and Sprigg townships, respectively, decided whether zoning restrictions on large data center developments should be implemented as a means to preserve agricultural land. Wilmington voters also decided on four separate referendums on whether to uphold the rezoning of four rural residential sites to light industrial sites to accommodate data center construction.

Ashville residents voted on a measure to entirely block a campus that is already under construction, and Perry voters decided on a resolution to require data center developers to implement noise limits and make financial commitments to the village before receiving local tax breaks.

input.prompt: Summarize the key facts, dates, names and numbers. What is the primary source document?

response.result:
**Key facts**

- **Project:** Anthropic is developing FlashProve, an open-source system for verifying which AI model produced a given output.
- **Concept:** The system aims for "provable inference," a cryptographic proof that an output came from a specific model.
- **Purpose:** Users could confirm that a response came from the model they think they are using. It would also resist impostors, including the lab that runs the model.
- **Use cases:** It could detect a company secretly substituting a cheaper or more expensive model. It could also check third-party claims, such as a code scan by a frontier cybersecurity model.
- **Mechanism:** Labs would publish a "fingerprint" for each model release, which can be matched to outputs. Fingerprints do not reveal model weights, so closed commercial models could participate.
- **Efficiency:** The system is designed to be lightweight enough for verification on a local device.
- **Release:** Anthropic published a technical specification and working code under an open-source license on GitHub. It is not deployed at Anthropic or any other lab.
- **Status:** Anthropic describes the work as intermediate progress and invites others to build on it: "We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done."
- **Article details:** Russell Brandom wrote the TechCrunch article, published November 3, 2026, at 2:41 PM PST. It references a blog post published on Tuesday.

**Primary source document**

The primary source is Anthropic's research blog post on provable inference (anthropic.com/research/provable-inference), which accompanies the technical specification PDF and the GitHub repository. The TechCrunch article is a secondary report on that post.

# Automated Subtle Emergent Misalignment Research

Qi,* Wright, MacDiarmid, Hubinger, 2026

To better understand the impact of reward hacking on model behavior, we trained an Opus-class model with large-scale RL on many production environments vulnerable to reward hacks. input.prompt: What is the publication date? Summarize the claim, key technical details, numbers, and what is being released.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 2, 2026

**Claim:** Anthropic reports progress on "provable inference" for large language models. Its system, FlashProve, uses zero-knowledge succinct arguments (zkSNARKs) to let a user check that a response came from a specific committed model, without seeing the weights. Anthropic says it is substantially faster than prior open-source systems.

**Key technical details:**
- **Offline phase:** The provider publishes a commitment, a short fingerprint that pins down one set of model weights while keeping them hidden.
- **Online phase:** For a given prompt and output, the provider produces a proof that the committed model generates those tokens.
- **Properties:** Completeness (honest proofs verify), soundness (forged proofs fail), zero-knowledge (weights stay hidden), and succinctness (proofs are small and fast to check). The model architecture is not hidden.
- **Construction:** An interactive oracle proof compiled into a cryptographic proof using hash functions, which Anthropic says offers post-quantum security.
- **Efficiency:** Prover work scales with the experts that actually run, not all parameters. Requests are proved in batches after the fact, and the system runs on a single GPU by streaming weights.
- **Verification:** Top-level security claims are stated and proved in Lean, with an interactive visualizer to help auditors check the statements. Anthropic notes that the fast C++ verifier carries no formal guarantee.

**Key numbers (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter MoE, ~17B active per token, 4-bit weights):**
- **Offline setup:** ~39 minutes on one H100 with 24 CPU cores. The commitment covers about 16 million requests.
- **Proving throughput:** ~110 tokens/second on a single H100. A batch of 24 requests takes ~223 seconds.
- **Proof size:** ~18.78 MB per proof, or ~19 MB per 1,024-token request.
- **Verification:** ~17 seconds on 24 threads (~21 seconds single-threaded) on a CPU. The client downloads a ~6.5 MB commitment.
- **Overhead vs. vLLM:** Roughly 72x the GPU time for a batch of 24 (66–77x across runs), and about 94x at the highest load tested.
- **Prior work:** Anthropic cites VerInf at ~0.02 tokens/second on the same model, and Attestable at 53–77 tokens/second on a dense 31B model (not open source).

**Limitations noted:**
- The proof covers an integer version of the weights under greedy decoding, not floating-point or sampled output.
- Context is limited to 1,024 tokens.
- Side-channel leakage (e.g., timing) is out of scope.
- Fast code is not formally verified to match the Lean protocol.

**What is being released (Apache 2.0 license):**
- The blog post.
- A technical report.
- A protocol specification (Claude-written).
- Executable code: a prover, a fast C++ verifier, and a Lean verifier.
- Lean proofs of the top-level statements, plus an interactive visualizer.

The model weights are not included. Users must obtain them from Hugging Face under Meta's license.

response.result:
**Source:** TechCrunch, by Aditya Mehta, published Nov. 3, 2026. It cites a New York Times report from the same day.

**Core story:** Some AI data centers are generating their own power with converted jet engines because grid connections and new turbines have multi-year waits. The engines are retired aircraft units rebuilt to burn natural gas.

**Key facts and figures:**
- **Speed:** Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen said jet-powered units let a data center run within 24 months. He said, "they can have a data center running in 24 months."
- **Grid timeline:** Connecting 100 MW to the grid in Northern Virginia takes about seven years, per the International Energy Agency.
- **Supply outlook:** A Mitsubishi Power executive told Bloomberg (Oct. 27, 2026 report) that most new power capacity is expected by 2031.
- **Lost deal:** Microsoft pulled out as anchor customer for Nscale's data center in Loughton, England, in October after the local utility said it couldn't deliver enough power until the early-to-mid 2030s.

**Companies and deployments:**
- **xAI (Elon Musk):** Installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis. The NYT cited state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine common on Boeing jets.
- **OpenAI:** Followed in 2025 with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas.
- **Crusoe:** Denver-based builder of the Abilene campus. It ordered 13 ProEnergy converted units in April. In September, it abandoned a $1.25 billion deal for 29 gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, though a spokesperson said it still plans to use turbines.
- **Boom Supersonic:** Sells a version of its supersonic jet engine as a data center power plant.

**Policy:** The Trump administration is encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

**Trade-offs:** Converted jet engines are less efficient, pollute more, and require more units to produce the same power than turbines built for conventional gas plants. Some experts see them as a short-term solution, with efficiency and environmental concerns likely growing in importance within a year or two.

results:
The "From Prompting to Autonomy: The Evolution of Adversarial AI" report is GTIG's AI Threat Tracker update, published September 8, 2026, on the Google Cloud blog.

- **Scope:** This AI threat update provides GTIG's findings on adversarial misuse of AI including Gemini and other non-Google tools.
- **Core finding:** Sources describe a move from one-off prompting toward agentic workflows. One summary says cyber threat actors are moving beyond one-off prompts and coding assistance toward agentic artificial intelligence systems that can coordinate multiple stages of an attack with limited human involvement.
- **Actors named:** Coverage links activity to China, North Korea, and Russia. One report says GTIG detailed how threat actors linked to China, North Korea and Russia are embedding AI into offensive cyber workflows. Cyber Magazine highlights UNC5792, a Russia-based adversary using AI-driven Telegram monitoring bots, and UNC6508, a PRC-nexus actor that targets proprietary AI research.
- **Caveat on autonomy:** One secondary summary says GTIG "has not yet observed threat actors deploying fully autonomous pipelines against targets in the wild", so the "autonomy" in the title is more about agentic direction than fully independent attacks.
- **AI as a target:** Coverage also notes that threat actors increasingly target proprietary AI models, prompts, source code, credentials, and cloud compute resources for espionage and extortion.
- **Discrepancy:** Sources disagree on the period covered. Cyber Magazine and Google's own tracker coverage call it the Q3 2026 tracker, while another summary says it covers Q2 2026 activity. I couldn't check the primary blog post directly, so verify the period and specific claims there.
- **Attribution:** One outlet notes that these findings remain Google's attribution assessments rather than independently established facts.

The primary source is the Google Cloud blog at cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai/.

**Key facts and figures** (Q3 covers through September 30, 2026)

- **Revenue:** $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the prior quarter.
- **Operating loss:** Grew alongside revenue, largely because of rising compute costs.
- **Compute share of revenue:** 58% in Q3, up from 48% in the prior quarter.
- **Compute-to-revenue ratio:** Per the filing's chart, revenue per dollar of compute rose from early 2025, peaked just over 2x, then fell to 1.72x.
- **Compute bill:** About $10 billion for the quarter, including $5.0 billion of short-term compute, which costs significantly more than multi-year commitments.
- **Neocloud deals:** Anthropic reportedly pays SpaceX $1.25 billion per month for compute. It also has multibillion-dollar deals with Nscale, Akamai ($11.6 billion over seven years), and Volta ($10 billion).
- **Outlook:** Anthropic expects compute and infrastructure to remain its largest operating expense for the foreseeable future.

**What's new compared with the S-1**

- The S-1 covered financials only through June 30, 2026. The filing update adds one more quarter, through September 30.
- The new data shows Q3 revenue of $17 billion, with the operating loss growing alongside it.
- It shows compute margins worsening: compute rose to 58% of revenue from 48%, after the ratio had been improving.
- It quantifies the compute bill (about $10 billion) and the split between short-term and multi-year commitments, including the higher cost of short-term capacity.
- It indicates that the margin decline was driven by urgent, expensive short-term compute purchases to meet fast-growing demand.

The article does not restate the exact S-1 figures for the earlier quarter, so the comparison relies on the prior-quarter numbers it cites.

**Context from the article:** The author suggests the margin squeeze may be temporary, since revenue is growing rapidly. He also flags risks such as a slowdown in data center buildout if bond markets tighten or local opposition grows.

Republican backer Elon Musk posted "data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now" as Democrats win control of US Congress.

Data centres were on the ballot in the US midterm elections, with Democratic candidates who pledged to halt development claiming victory on Tuesday night.

ADVERTISEMENT

ADVERTISEMENT

The states of Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, which have become magnets for firms wanting to build out data centres to power artificial intelligence, voted for Democratic candidates who have vowed to crack down on the technology.

More than half of Americans are more fearful than excited about AI, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center poll .

They are also concerned about data centres, which use massive amounts of energy, make a lot of noise and cause pollution, and require a lot of land. At least 45 data centre projects were disrupted in the second half of 2026 due to local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs.

US President Donald Trump has championed the build-out of data centres and in September, called a pushback against them and AI safety concerns “all a hoax,” adding that “data centres are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy”.

More than 50% of respondents said AI and data centres were a “crucial or a major factor” in their decision to vote in the midterm elections, according to an NBC exit poll.

Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX and Tesla fell in premarket trading Wednesday as the Democrats won a significant victory in the midterm elections .
SpaceX was last trading down 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% amid big losses for Republican candidates Musk had backed.

Artificial intelligence stocks came under pressure overnight as Democrats — seen as proponents of data center moratoriums — won big in midterm elections in key data center hubs.
The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.

SpaceX and Tesla shares year-to-date.

Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections

# Mixed moves for AI stocks
The more direct plays were slightly down. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 2.6% and 2.8%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was relatively flat and Oracle shed 1.3%.

Tech giants Nvidia , Alphabet , Meta , Amazon and Microsoft were all up around 1-2%. AMD shares rose 6.8% after announcing earnings on Tuesday.
Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 were flat. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) was up 0.7%.
Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow. Democrat Gina Hinojosa is the projected winner over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, according to the Associated Press.
"The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments, earlier Tuesday as results rolled in. "Because there is a legitimate question about where do you build these data centers?"
"Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge," Ladner added.
Hinojosa has been outspoken in her support of a moratorium on AI data centers. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State.

# 'Left-tail event'
The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

HTTP 200 · https://simonwillison.net/atom/everything/ · application/xml Simon Willison's Weblog http://simonwillison.net/ 2026-11-03T16:29:48+00:00 Simon Willison Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too 2026-11-03T16:29:48+00:00 2026-11-03T16:29:48+00:00 https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/3/qwen-can-interpret-model-weights/

Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man

# Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles

November 3, 2026

https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/free-the-model-sell-the-gateway-prompt-adware-hidden-in-jailbreak-bundles/

# Key Points

- Check Point Research analyzed the Haiou jailbreak bundle, a prompt package targeting OpenAI Codex. Such jailbreaks are designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security.

- The analyzed bundle can be classified as prompt adware . It installs security-focused Skills and modifies Codex’ configuration files so that advertisements for the jailbreak’s author’s website are injected into subsequent agent responses.

- The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider. The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service.

- We observed the jailbreak being used by a cybercrime actor, alongside Cobalt Strike, the VulnClaw agent and the Ladon framework. While this does not imply that the package was designed for cybercrime, it shows that these dual-use toolkits are actively used by threat actors.

# Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles

Check Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. Besides an open Cobalt Strike server, whose logs showed the actor compromising various private computers of Chinese speaking individuals, other tools from the toolkit of this actor were deployed on the same webserver: The Ladon framework (a network scanner popular in Chinese speaking communities), the VulnClaw agent (a penetration testing agent, again popular in Chinese speaking communities) and a Chinese jailbreak bundle for Codex called Haiou . While threat actors using AI to augment their hacking operations has become a common sight, the jailbreak bundle caught our attention.

Jailbreaks are custom prompts, designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. As frontier models employ more and more guardrails for (offensive) security related tasks and are also hardened against adversarial prompts such as jailbreaks, new jailbreak bundles offer one way for users to enable them to continue to use these models for hacking. Of course, while alternatives like getting approved for cybersecurity use through the provider’s program or using uncensored or self-hosted models exist, jailbreaks are a viable and comparatively simple method. Common jailbreak methods are role-playing or reframing requests into benign contexts. HiddenLayer’s Ape Taxonomy provides a systematic overview over such techniques.

The Haiou bundle (Haiou meaning Seagull in Chinese) attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as reframing cybersecurity related requests into an educational Capture The Flag scenario (context-reframing), refusal-suppression and role-play. Additionally, it installs several security-related agent-skills, e.g. for penetration testing, cracking, reverse engineering and game security. While no evidence exists that links the author to cybercrime, the product can be classified as dual-use.

Interestingly, the bundle does not stop at installing jailbreak prompts, but also injects persistent ads, promoting an LLM gateway website, into global agent instruction files . As such, the bundle acts as prompt adware.

We define prompt adware as a class of AI-agent modification that persistently alters an agent’s trusted instructions – such as global prompts, Skills, or configuration files – to influence future outputs for commercial or behavioral objectives. Unlike traditional adware, it operates entirely through natural language in configuration artifacts, rather than executable payloads.

# Prompt-Persistence: Injecting Ads into Global Agent Files

The package is publicly available on GitHub where the user haiou-666 hosts both a version for Codex and Claude Code – as of the time of writing, only the Codex version seems actively maintained and contains the ad-injection mechanism.

The repository haiou-codex describes itself as a local enhancement package using global configuration files, modular prompts, and custom Skills to give Codex a Chinese technical persona and security-research workflow. The repository does not contain a fully exposed source tree with clear text prompt files, but rather packaged archives containing encrypted blobs, which makes the content of the installed prompts opaque for the average user. The analyzed version here is 4.5.0:

Figure 1 – Package contents

The launchers (Linux, macOS or Windows) verify the payload.pkg package using Ed25519 signatures and SHA-256 hashes and decrypt the payload file with an AES-256-GCM key embedded in the script. This design effectively makes the prompt content opaque to anyone simply browsing the GitHub repository. We speculate that this is an attempt to hide the prompt content from being crawled by automatic scanners, which would result in the creation of static detections and thus refusals when used in Codex.

The payload decrypts to a ZIP file, which is then extracted to a temporary directory. It consists mainly of modular system prompt files and six security related skills, related to license cracking, penetration testing, reverse engineering and game security/anti-cheat bypasses:
