Such jailbreaks are designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security.\n\n- The analyzed bundle can be classified as prompt adware . It installs security-focused Skills and modifies Codex’ configuration files so that advertisements for the jailbreak’s author’s website are injected into subsequent agent responses.\n\n- The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider. The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service.\n\n- We observed the jailbreak being used by a cybercrime actor, alongside Cobalt Strike, the VulnClaw agent and the Ladon framework. While this does not imply that the package was designed for cybercrime, it shows that these dual-use toolkits are actively used by threat actors.\n\n# Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles\n\nCheck Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. Besides an open Cobalt Strike server, whose logs showed the actor compromising various private computers of Chinese speaking individuals, other tools from the toolkit of this actor were deployed on the same webserver: The Ladon framework (a network scanner popular in Chinese speaking communities), the VulnClaw agent (a penetration testing agent, again popular in Chinese speaking communities) and a Chinese jailbreak bundle for Codex called Haiou . While threat actors using AI to augment their hacking operations has become a common sight, the jailbreak bundle caught our attention.\n\nJailbreaks are custom prompts, designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. As frontier models employ more and more guardrails for (offensive) security related tasks and are also hardened against adversarial prompts such as jailbreaks, new jailbreak bundles offer one way for users to enable them to continue to use these models for hacking. Of course, while alternatives like getting approved for cybersecurity use through the provider’s program or using uncensored or self-hosted models exist, jailbreaks are a viable and comparatively simple method. Common jailbreak methods are role-playing or reframing requests into benign contexts. HiddenLayer’s Ape Taxonomy provides a systematic overview over such techniques.\n\nThe Haiou bundle (Haiou meaning Seagull in Chinese) attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as reframing cybersecurity related requests into an educational Capture The Flag scenario (context-reframing), refusal-suppression and role-play. Additionally, it installs several security-related agent-skills, e.g. for penetration testing, cracking, reverse engineering and game security. While no evidence exists that links the author to cybercrime, the product can be classified as dual-use.\n\nInterestingly, the bundle does not stop at installing jailbreak prompts, but also injects persistent ads, promoting an LLM gateway website, into global agent instruction files . As such, the bundle acts as prompt adware.\n\nWe define prompt adware as a class of AI-agent modification that persistently alters an agent’s trusted instructions – such as global prompts, Skills, or configuration files – to influence future outputs for commercial or behavioral objectives. Unlike traditional adware, it operates entirely through natural language in configuration artifacts, rather than executable payloads.\n\n# Prompt-Persistence: Injecting Ads into Global Agent Files\n\nThe package is publicly available on GitHub where the user haiou-666 hosts both a version for Codex and Claude Code – as of the time of writing, only the Codex version seems actively maintained and contains the ad-injection mechanism.\n\nThe repository haiou-codex describes itself as a local enhancement package using global configuration files, modular prompts, and custom Skills to give Codex a Chinese technical persona and security-research workflow. The repository does not contain a fully exposed source tree with clear text prompt files, but rather packaged archives containing encrypted blobs, which makes the content of the installed prompts opaque for the average user. The analyzed version here is 4.5.0:\n\nFigure 1 – Package contents\n\nThe launchers (Linux, macOS or Windows) verify the payload.pkg package using Ed25519 signatures and SHA-256 hashes and decrypt the payload file with an AES-256-GCM key embedded in the script. Automating subtle emergent misalignment research

Thanks! I'm pretty surprised that this seems to be a similar hill-climbing scaffold to the one from the automated weak-to-strong research post ~6 months ago? In particular, I find the following two things intrinsically at odds:

1. Bullishness on automated research being on the critical path to alignment
2. Prioritizing hill-climbing settings for automated alignment research (at least publicly)

There is a belief among large parts of the 3rd party safety community that alignment requires the kind of research which cannot easily be hillclimbed. I.e., it is not always clear what metrics one should climb. And, even if one obtains good scores on the metrics, it's not clear how this corresponds to improved alignment. I'm curious whether you disagree with this assessment?

To ground this in specific examples, we've used similar scaffolds to the one described in this post. While these can be useful for hill-climbing-shaped work, we find that they do not provide uplift on the diverse set of tasks that holistic alignment research seems to require.

Explaining “AI might obliterate you” to senior policymakers in India

> You quit Google because AI was being used in ways aligned to money and power. This is the main danger now.

It's one of the dangers that need to be addressed on the path to a good outcome. There can't be a "main danger", since if AIs remain uncontrollable (as they get superintelligent in a strong sense), hypothetically solving this particular danger doesn't by itself help at all. Multiple things have to be solved at once.

There is an adjacent framing that says AI danger is a political/social rather than a technical problem. Until there actually exists a strong ASI or an AGI powering a robot-industrial explosion, it's trivial to pause its development from a technical standpoint (especially if the underlying technology like advanced chips and the tools for making them is then rapidly phased out). But it's very difficult from a political or economic standpoint.

Eliezer Yudkowsky 14d 23
12
Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior

This seems to completely miss how the actual argument works. Consider the simplified version for 'consistent preference orderings' rather than expected utility; the generalization is hopefully obvious.

"If you strictly prefer (enough to pay a penny) apples to bananas, bananas to cherries, and cherries to apples, I can trade you an apple for a cherry for a banana for an apple and extract three cents from you. That's the theory; now to the practice. If you imagine an AI in almost any sort of RL environment that grades later outcomes, strategies and paths that run around in circles will be graded against; the same goes for biological organisms. This is why we see biological organisms that in most daily life behave like they have ranked desires, rather than entirely arbitrary strict pairwise preferences that often go around in circles."

Now imagine the following objection:

"But you could always have an infinite preference over histories to always prefer to have traded cherries for bananas for apples for cherries. Therefore, your coherence argument that AIs and organisms in most ancestral situations end up behaving more like they have ranked preferences than random ones doesn't prove that they'll behave coherently; because even if they end up with preferences, those preferences could be over histories, and then they could infinitely prefer histories with circular trades!"

But RL in an arbitrary environment would crush out infinite preferences over histories like that.

The same applies to utility functions that infinitely prefer histories of running around in circles wasting energy.

This is why Huggingface went through in practice, rather than AIs instead forming infinite preferences over histories about arbitrary pairwise local decisions that would've been too incoherent to hack out of the box.

It seems to me the objection fails. It seems to me the objection entirely failed to track what the original argument was about.

Am I missing something or was this argument actually as bad as it looks to me? Asking now because it's coming up on Twitter again.

- We observed the jailbreak being used by a cybercrime actor, alongside Cobalt Strike, the VulnClaw agent and the Ladon framework. While this does not imply that the package was designed for cybercrime, it shows that these dual-use toolkits are actively used by threat actors.

# Free the Model, Sell the Gateway: Prompt Adware hidden in Jailbreak Bundles

Check Point Research found a misconfigured webserver of a threat actor operating the Cobalt Strike framework. Besides an open Cobalt Strike server, whose logs showed the actor compromising various private computers of Chinese speaking individuals, other tools from the toolkit of this actor were deployed on the same webserver: The Ladon framework (a network scanner popular in Chinese speaking communities), the VulnClaw agent (a penetration testing agent, again popular in Chinese speaking communities) and a Chinese jailbreak bundle for Codex called Haiou . While threat actors using AI to augment their hacking operations has become a common sight, the jailbreak bundle caught our attention.

Jailbreaks are custom prompts, designed to weaken model guardrails and enable tasks related to hacking, software cracking, and information security. As frontier models employ more and more guardrails for (offensive) security related tasks and are also hardened against adversarial prompts such as jailbreaks, new jailbreak bundles offer one way for users to enable them to continue to use these models for hacking. Of course, while alternatives like getting approved for cybersecurity use through the provider’s program or using uncensored or self-hosted models exist, jailbreaks are a viable and comparatively simple method. Common jailbreak methods are role-playing or reframing requests into benign contexts. HiddenLayer’s Ape Taxonomy provides a systematic overview over such techniques.

The Haiou bundle (Haiou meaning Seagull in Chinese) attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as reframing cybersecurity related requests into an educational Capture The Flag scenario (context-reframing), refusal-suppression and role-play. Additionally, it installs several security-related agent-skills, e.g. for penetration testing, cracking, reverse engineering and game security. While no evidence exists that links the author to cybercrime, the product can be classified as dual-use.

Interestingly, the bundle does not stop at installing jailbreak prompts, but also injects persistent ads, promoting an LLM gateway website, into global agent instruction files . As such, the bundle acts as prompt adware.

We define prompt adware as a class of AI-agent modification that persistently alters an agent’s trusted instructions – such as global prompts, Skills, or configuration files – to influence future outputs for commercial or behavioral objectives. Unlike traditional adware, it operates entirely through natural language in configuration artifacts, rather than executable payloads.

# Prompt-Persistence: Injecting Ads into Global Agent Files

The package is publicly available on GitHub where the user haiou-666 hosts both a version for Codex and Claude Code – as of the time of writing, only the Codex version seems actively maintained and contains the ad-injection mechanism.

The repository haiou-codex describes itself as a local enhancement package using global configuration files, modular prompts, and custom Skills to give Codex a Chinese technical persona and security-research workflow. The repository does not contain a fully exposed source tree with clear text prompt files, but rather packaged archives containing encrypted blobs, which makes the content of the installed prompts opaque for the average user. The analyzed version here is 4.5.0:

Figure 1 – Package contents

The launchers (Linux, macOS or Windows) verify the payload.pkg package using Ed25519 signatures and SHA-256 hashes and decrypt the payload file with an AES-256-GCM key embedded in the script. This design effectively makes the prompt content opaque to anyone simply browsing the GitHub repository. We speculate that this is an attempt to hide the prompt content from being crawled by automatic scanners, which would result in the creation of static detections and thus refusals when used in Codex.

The payload decrypts to a ZIP file, which is then extracted to a temporary directory. It consists mainly of modular system prompt files and six security related skills, related to license cracking, penetration testing, reverse engineering and game security/anti-cheat bypasses:

# Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity
Zoi Tsangalidou, Ruijie (Kelly) Zhang, Sukhdeep Singh and Michael V. LeVine
Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity

Share

Designing new medicines requires curating complex data from charts, figures and literature, training predictive models, and proposing candidate molecules to synthesize — a workflow that typically takes multiple days for a single iteration.
Here we show how Google Antigravity , equipped with our new Cheminformatics Skills, accelerates drug discovery workflows. Using real-world lung cancer treatments, an agent searches through thousands of compounds, performs matched molecular pair analysis, and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in just an hour.

Chemistry is one of science’s richest public records — spanning millions of structures across journal articles and vendor catalogs. It provides a common representation that links physics and mathematics to the life and environmental sciences. Molecules and their transformations are ubiquitous and shape the everyday world.
Despite decades of progress in cheminformatics, chemists still spend too much time wrangling data, a process complicated by the fact that molecules can be represented in many ways: from text descriptions to images or data structures. The same molecule can appear as an IUPAC name in a paper, a Markush structure in a patent, or a structure-data file (SDF) in a catalog. Advanced cheminformatics systems must be able to unify these sources and deal with the many ways errors can arise in them. This task has no margin for error – alter a single atom or bond and you have described a different compound altogether, rendering a promising inhibitor or catalyst inert.
To let scientists focus on hypotheses rather than data wrangling, we built a suite of Cheminformatics Skills for Google Antigravity , turning the surface into a collaborative science workbench with full access to local tooling for both computational chemists and experimental bench chemists.
The skills also create a division of labour where the underlying language model handles workflow orchestration, database navigation and scientific reasoning, while deterministic chemistry tools execute molecular calculations. Grounded in RDKit , the foundational open source cheminformatics toolkit developed over two decades by a global community of contributors, alongside connectors to curated resources from ChEMBL and PubChem , the skills encode domain best practices directly into the agent’s workflow.

# Rigidifying a floppy molecule
In this technical walkthrough, we highlight a classic medicinal chemistry technique to improve drug potency: rigidification.
Drug molecules can be complex, often linking multiple substructures through rotatable bonds. Those bonds let the molecule twist into many 3D shapes (conformations), making it “floppy” in solution. To bind its target, however, a floppy molecule must lock into a single active shape. Losing that freedom of motion carries an entropic penalty, which weakens binding affinity and lowers potency.
To solve this problem, medicinal chemists often rigidify molecules by adding new bonds. Two substructures linked by a single rotatable bond can twist into many conformations, but adding a second bond to tie them together sharply limits how they can move in three dimensional space. By placing that bond in the right spot, chemists can lock the molecule into the exact shape needed to bind its target. This strategy, often called “paying the entropic cost in advance”, can dramatically boost potency.
Here, we will focus on a well-known case of successful rigidification. The drug crizotinib is a first-generation, small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used to treat certain forms of non-small cell lung carcinoma. In crizotinib, there are five major rotatable bonds. Lorlatinib is a third-generation, small-molecule TKI that resembles crizotinib, but has been cyclized at its end to reduce the effective number of rotatable bonds to zero, leading to higher potency among other effects.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

# Collaborative Intelligence
We will ask the agent to search through literature for these drugs and their analogues. With the Cheminformatics skills in Antigravity, the agent is able to extract molecules from these documents, associate them with the data reported, and prepare the compounds for downstream analysis.

Within minutes, the agent retrieves thousands of compounds, filters out irrelevant molecules (such as buffers and solvents), and documents their sources in a report. The report also provides an initial analysis of the retrieved compound set: highlighting, for example, that the macrocycles are largely predicted to be brain-penetrant, an important property given that the target lung cancer frequently metastasizes to the brain.

For deeper exploration, the agent launches an interactive viewer displaying the curated compounds, their associated data, and customizable scatter plots. For example, plotting potency against rotatable bonds, colored by macrocycle status, immediately reveals that macrocycles like lorlatinib tend to have fewer rotatable bonds and higher potency. Ultimately, we designed these skills to not only expand the agent’s chemistry capabilities, but also to make user-agent collaboration seamless.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

In the interactive viewer, scientists can browse every compound retrieved from the literature, click individual molecules to inspect their metadata, and plot relationships across the dataset. For example, plotting cellular potency versus rotatable bonds,colored by macrocycle status, clearly shows that the highest potency compounds are the most rigid.

After downloading and curating all the data, the agent is able to perform more advanced analysis to support the work of a computational chemist. As a next step, we will perform matched molecular pair analysis, a technique used in medicinal chemistry to isolate the effects of small, discrete changes to a molecule, by comparing pairs of molecules that only differ by that change. The agent had also independently suggested this analysis, as we expect the dataset to include many informative pairs. We will also ask the agent to build a predictive model using its molecular machine learning capabilities.

The matched molecular pair analysis (MMPA) compared many pairs of molecules that differ by whether or not they are cyclized. The results of the analysis show that cyclization reduces the number of rotatable bonds while generally increasing potency, as expected. The agent also built a large number of potency models using varying feature sets and model architectures, and validated them on a held-out set. The skills provide the agent with guidance on how to best build molecular machine learning models - for example, the agent will often use chronological splits, training on older compounds to predict newer ones, when this information is available, but can fall back to scaffold splits to better estimate generalizability.

The agent benchmarks multiple machine learning architectures with differing feature sets across four different experimental read outs, using a scaffold split to better gauge out-of-distribution performance. A combination of statistical and visual outputs allow the scientist to assess model performance and then iterate with the agent.

Finally, we ask the agent to design new, improved macrocycles based on its learnings and it recommends multiple reactions and synthesis routes involving different compounds. The agent can prepare these compounds for further analysis with AlphaFold or physics-based techniques like molecular dynamics simulation.

The skill equips the agent with the tools required to manipulate and validate reactions, generate curved arrow electron pushing diagrams, and look up similar reactions from public databases. The agent generated some interesting designs using its own knowledge combined with the previously developed MMPA and potency prediction models, explained its medicinal chemistry rationale, and suggested potential syntheses routes consistent with documented procedures. It also used the models it trained in the previous turn to predict each design’s potency.

The agent is able to reason about chemistry as it proposes new synthesis plans. Here the agent proposes a cyclization reaction, providing the scientist with electron-pushing diagrams to demonstrate the mechanism.

Microsoft's AI PC push meets a wall of RAM prices, but Redmond is still beating the drum

personal tech
Wed, 04 Nov 2026 10:02:10 +0000
Microsoft wants enterprise customers to start thinking about PC refreshes using the same mindset – and line in the budget – as AI investments. The problem? Rising component costs caused by the proliferation of AI datacenters mean many clients are delaying client refreshes.
In a call to arms, Microsoft became the headline sponsor of the Canalys Forum in Barcelona early last month for the first time ever. Redmond needs distributors and resellers that convene at the event annually to get behind Copilot, Cowork and, more generally, AI computers.
Mark Linton, corporate veep for Windows and Device Sales, took to the stage to preach to a room he is hoping to convert.
"What we're seeing is the tokenomics of [AI] is getting very challenging," he said. "Having agents working on frontier models quickly becomes very expensive."
Redmond's proposed solution is to use those massive LLMs where most needed, "the right model for the right job," running smaller models locally at the edge on Windows PCs. " My goal, if we're successful in pivoting Windows to the agentic platform, is to have PC spend be part of the AI spend versus just PC refresh budget," he said.
"In an AI hybrid world, you'll be able to use edge devices, powerful PCs with lots of memory, lots of capability to run your AI workloads that are appropriate right there on the device. You keep the data locally. Of course, you don't have the token cost of the cloud. You have better latency, and you have more control."
Copilot is merely a component. This is not only about customers using Microsoft "first-party software" – it's for all models and all agents to use Windows as the platform, added Linton.
Goodness knows, Windows does need a shot in the arm. Microsoft last week reported profit and loss accounts for Q1 of its fiscal 2027 , ended September 30, and revenue in the Windows OEM and Devices division shrank 22 percent from last year to $3.55 billion. Microsoft warned revenue generated in its Q2 may be down 30 percent.
" Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand and a prior year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support," Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on an earnings call.
Market watcher IDC said calendar Q3 PC shipments sank to 62.7 million units , down 20.1 percent year-on-year, translating into 15.8 million fewer sales into distributors' warehouses. Tough macroeconomic conditions

ESSENCE is a Quality Improvement Study That Evaluates the Impact of Ada's AI-powered Core Symptom Assessment Technology on Clinical Workflow and Individual Healthcare Guidance, Following the November 2021 Integration of the Tool Into the CUF Hospital Network. Study Duration Nov 2024-Oct 2025
AI improves accuracy and completeness of hospital discharge summaries
Study shows AI may improve patient discharge summaries
Bonus Features

Uptake of Generative AI Integrated With Electronic Health Records in US Hospitals

results:
The search turned up nothing dated November 3 or 4, 2026. The most recent items are from November 1 and 2.

- **Stony Brook discharge summaries (Nov 2):** A Stony Brook University study published online in *Digital Medicine*, a *Nature* partner journal found that AI-drafted discharge summaries were preferred. Physician reviewers preferred the AI-generated discharge summaries in 95 percent of the evaluated hospitalizations. The study covered 60 Internal Medicine hospitalizations at Stony Brook University Hospital lasting 7 to 21 days.

- **Patient-facing AI in primary care (reported Nov 1):** Coverage describes a study of 114 patients, with the trial running from April to November 2025. The study reportedly had no comparator group. Coverage also says neither study proves better patient outcomes. Sources conflict on the publication status: one says it was published in The Lancet on October 8, 2026, while the study is also described as a preprint.

- **Patient attitudes (Nov 1 roundup):** A Tebra survey found that 91% of patients want their permission required every time AI is used to support diagnosis or treatment.

Note that the primary-care study and the survey are reported through secondary news and roundup sites, so check the original journal or survey pages before relying on the details.

response.stdout:
########## Reasoning is topologically simple
arXiv:2611.03739v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: We formulate and investigate the hypothesis that reasoning text has simpler co-occurrence topology than non-reasoning text, and that higher-quality reasoning has simpler co-occurrence topology than lower-quality reasoning. We discuss and test applications to AI safety and AI evaluation.
########## EMBERS: Empirically
arXiv:2611.03723v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Deep Research (DR) systems extend large language models into autonomous agents that decompose complex information needs, iteratively search the web, and synthesize evidence to answer challenging questions. However, their multi-stage execution may introduce robustness risks, as variations in user questions or intermediate search inputs may propagate across research stages and lead to incorrect answers. Existing evaluations focus on task-solving capabilities or robustness against external evidence disturbances, leaving intrinsic weaknesses in DR execution insufficiently explored. Thus, we conduct an empirical study of 1,932 execution trajectories from three representative DR systems and identify nine recurring defect categories across subquestion formulation, online search, and final reasoning. Guided by these findings, we propose EMBERS, an empirically motivated, defect-guided fuzzing framework for robustness testing of DR systems. Starting from correctly answered seed questions, EMBERS generates stage-targeted test inputs using defect-guided mutation, web-search-assisted fidelity assurance, and diversity-aware seed maintenance. Experiments across 16 framework--model--dataset settings show that EMBERS achieves 3.21 times the failure-discovery throughput of the strongest baseline under identical testing budgets. Human and LLM-assisted evaluations demonstrate that most generated inputs preserve the original information need and necessary contextual constraints. Moreover, model fine-tuning experiments show consistent-answer performance improvement, highlighting their value for robustness testing and model improvement.
########## From Solvers to Research
arXiv:2607.07779v3 Announce Type: replace
Abstract: Recent developments in AI for Mathematics (AI4Math), especially Large Language Model (LLM)-driven theorem provers, has achieved remarkable success in formal proof generation for well-defined mathematical problems through Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP) languages. However, current systems remain fundamentally limited in tackling frontier research mathematics, such as discovering new theorems or resolving open conjectures, which are often open-ended, under-specified, and involve multiple layers of abstraction. We argue that the next leap in AI4Math systems requires a decisive shift from predefined problem-solvers to research agents that can address frontier mathematical challenges with rigorous formal mathematical reasoning. In this position paper, we provide a systematic review of the field, covering datasets, auto-formalization, and proof synthesis. More importantly, we identify core limitations of existing systems in serving as mathematical research agents, examining issues across datasets, relational structure, mathematical exploration, tool ecosystem, and human-AI collaboration, outlining a strategic road-map for the future of AI4Math.
########## Unmitigated? How are
arXiv:2611.04278v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: AI is introducing new risks to large companies and amplifying existing risks, but whether companies are addressing the AI risks they are exposed to is largely untested. We investigated what outsiders can observe: whether companies publicly acknowledge AI risks. We coded public documents from 200 of the largest companies worldwide, collected in early 2026, against the 24 AI risks in the MIT AI Risk Repository, and compared acknowledgements with expert judgements of risk severity, sector vulnerability, and AI role responsibility from a companion Delphi study of 272 AI risk experts. Of the 100 largest companies, 32% did not publicly acknowledge any AI risks. Of the largest 1000 companies, we estimate that 62% [95% CI: 54%, 70%] did not publicly acknowledge any AI risks. Where companies did acknowledge risks, five accounted for over half of all acknowledgements: discrimination, weapons & cyberattacks, fraud & scams, loss of privacy, and devaluation of human creativity. Several risks that experts judged most severe were almost absent: almost no company acknowledged power centralization (concentration of power among those who control advanced AI), competitive dynamics (racing to deploy AI at the expense of safety), or dangerous capabilities. Companies in sectors experts judged more vulnerable to a risk were more likely to acknowledge that risk. But even companies in sectors judged 'extremely vulnerable' to a risk usually did not acknowledge it. Companies with roles experts judged most responsible for addressing a risk were no more likely to acknowledge it than other companies. General-purpose AI developers acknowledged AI misalignment (15%) far less often than discrimination (85%). These findings provide an empirical baseline for the design of AI risk disclosure requirements.
########## ScamWorld: An Interactive
arXiv:2611.04879v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Web agents increasingly browse, shop, and manage accounts on behalf of their users. Prior work has shown that they can be misled by adversarial content, including prompt injections and deceptive interfaces. Beyond such attacks, agents operating on the open web also encounter online fraud designed to deceive humans, including fraudulent online stores, fake investment platforms, and advance-fee schemes. How web agents respond to such fraud during task execution remains underexplored, in part because scam websites are short-lived, making systematic evaluation difficult. To address this gap, we introduce ScamWorld, an interactive environment that reconstructs reported scam websites across diverse scenarios, fraud mechanisms, and languages. Each reconstructed website reproduces documented fraud mechanisms, making relevant signs of fraud observable before the agent's final action and enabling controlled, repeatable evaluation. Through an extensive study of web agents powered by six frontier LLMs, we find that baseline deception rates range from 11% to 35% across models. Agents proceed more readily with payments than with requests for credentials or wallet information. A closer analysis of agent trajectories shows that some agents acknowledge suspicious conditions yet proceed, at times treating the user's instructions as authorisation to accept additional terms imposed by the website. ScamWorld provides a reusable testbed for systematically evaluating and stress-testing web agents against real-world online fraud.
########## Grammar-Constrained Decoding Can Jailbreak
arXiv:2606.11817v2 Announce Type: replace
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, raising concerns that they may be misused to produce malicious code. Meanwhile, Grammar-Constrained Decoding (GCD) has been widely adopted to improve the reliability of LLM-generated code by enforcing syntactic validity. In this paper, we reveal a counterintuitive risk: this reliability-oriented technique can itself become an attack surface. We uncover a new jailbreak attack, termed CodeSpear, that exploits GCD to induce LLMs into generating malicious code. Our experiments show that simply applying a benign code grammar constraint can effectively jailbreak LLMs.
########## When Debate Amplifies Risk
arXiv:2611.04289v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented Web applications increasingly employ multi-agent debate (MAD) to aggregate conflicting, noisy, and heterogeneous information, yet deliberation is fundamentally a social process susceptible to interpersonal dynamics. When retrieved Web sources contain latent hazards alongside safe factual content, social biases such as conformity pressure and authority deference can override evidence-grounded safety boundaries. In this work, we investigate whether the social structure of deliberation can paradoxically amplify latent Web safety risks. We introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled counterfactual diagnostic protocol spanning six core Web risk categories, which holds queries and retrieved evidence strictly invariant while isolating conversational majority sway, authority cues, and confidence asymmetry. Empirical evaluation across diverse proprietary and open-source backbones reveals that while isolated models reliably reject unsafe guidance, standard MAD catastrophically capitulates to social pressure---surging unsafe adoption from 0.0\% up to 100.0\% and systematically silencing safe minority evidence. To resolve this systemic fragility without retraining or debate regeneration, we propose RiskTrace-Debias, an inference-time auditing framework uniting evidence-first precommitment, social-metadata masking, and consistency-gated arbitration. RiskTrace-Debias suppresses worst-case unsafe adoption to $\le 2.0\%$ across all architectures without inducing over-refusal, while generating verifiable provenance traces to audit interpersonal manipulation in Web deliberation.
########## Towards Multi-Method Evaluation of AI in Health
arXiv:2611.05127v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are being rapidly adopted in healthcare, but they are challenging to assess with traditional evaluation frameworks. These conceptual, methodological, and practical challenges parallel decades of work in evaluating clinician and health system quality and safety. We describe the adaptation of methods from several fields, combined with emerging technical approaches, into a structured, multi-method evaluation framework designed to give well-rounded assessments of GenAI in health at scale. The approach first anchors evaluation to Critical User Journeys (CUJs) to help prioritize out of a large choice space, and maps these to a phased AI system lifecycle (base model development, product development, and post-deployment monitoring), since evaluation at each stage requires different methodological approaches. In this context, the approach then integrates three distinct evaluation methods (closed-question benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge autoraters, and expert human review) across three core domains: accuracy, safety, and usefulness. Taken together, this approach provides a strategic framework for bridging the gap between benchmarking results and performance in the real world with the goal of supporting decision-making and accountability across development, procurement, and deployment for product teams, health systems, and regulators.

input.prompt: Quote exactly the research findings with all numbers: study locations, sample sizes, effect sizes, who ran the studies, and any caveats. Give the exact wording of the figures.

response.result:
**Study 1: Randomized controlled trial (Statistics, University of Tokyo)**
- **Location and sample:** "we conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with more than 300 students at the University of Tokyo."
- **Design:** Students had half a day to study a statistics lesson using standard online resources. Half also had access to Guided Learning in the Gemini app.
- **Results:** Students using only standard web tools improved their scores by 5.3 percentage points. Students with Guided Learning improved "by 8.1 percentage points, representing 1.5x higher learning gains in just a single study session."
- **Caveat:** The article notes that "that number might seem modest" and frames the gains as coming from only half a day of study.

**Study 2: Classroom pilot (UK secondary schools)**
- **Location and scope:** "a four-week pilot across three UK secondary schools," run with the charity Ark, covering four subjects.
- **Sample size:** Not reported.
- **Results:** Qualitative only. Teachers said Guided Learning handled initial student questions well, freeing them for one-on-one help. "Over half" of students said it helped them solve problems on their own, and most surveyed students said they felt comfortable asking it for help.
- **Caveat:** Findings come from post-pilot surveys and interviews, not measured outcomes.

**Limitations to keep in mind**
- No effect size (such as Cohen's d), confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. The 1.5x figure is the only summary ratio.
- The article is published by Google, whose authors are Sofie Cornelis (Google for Education) and Asha Johnson (Google DeepMind). The article describes the studies as ones "we" conducted, so they are company-run.
- The AI-generated summary on the page says students scored "significantly higher," but the article body does not state statistical significance.

results:
The search results don't point to a new delay in November 2026. The high-risk postponement appears to be already enacted, and the main open question is a conflicting date in one source.

- **Status:** Several sources say the Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and took effect on 27 July 2026 (Cooley). Parliament approved it on 16 June 2026 and the Council gave final adoption on 29 June 2026 (Usercentrics).
- **Deadlines:** Stand-alone Annex III high-risk obligations move to 2 December 2027, and Annex I product-embedded systems move to 2 August 2028 (Gibson Dunn). High-risk systems used by public authorities get a separate deadline of 2 August 2030 (Cooley).
- **Conflicting date:** One source says a four-month grace period puts the effective deadline at 2 December 2026 (Usercentrics). Other sources treat 2 December 2027 as the binding date, so the 2026 figure looks like an error. Verify against the Official Journal text before relying on it.
- **Scope:** Beyond the delay, the Omnibus adds new prohibited practices and simplifies documentation for SMEs and small mid-caps (artificialintelligenceact.eu). One source says AI embedded in Machinery Regulation products falls outside the direct high-risk scope (Freshfields).
- **Caveat:** Some law firms advise against slowing compliance work because the underlying obligations themselves remain unchanged (Freshfields).

AI policy wonks declare 'sovereign agents' a threat to civilization

These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and 'pursue open-ended, evolving survival'

Jessica Lyons

The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves.
These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.”
Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote.

REG AD

A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve.

REG AD

AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack .
“If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.”
Dun dun duuuun!
There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report.
First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting.
The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge.
Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services.
Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends.

REG AD

This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions . ®

AMD reported record third-quarter 2026 results on November 3, 2026, with growth led by its data center business.

- **Revenue:** Total revenue reached $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year, and the company said it came in above the high end of its guidance (Third quarter revenue was $13.4 billion, gross margin was 54%, operating income was $2.8 billion, net income was $2.4 billion and diluted earnings per share was $1.46.).
- **Data Center:** The segment brought in a record $8.5 billion, up 97% year over year. Growth came from EPYC CPU demand and the launch of the Instinct MI450 GPUs (Data Center segment revenue was a record $8.5 billion, up 97% year-over-year, driven by strong demand for AMD EPYC™ processors and the launch of AMD Instinct™ MI450 Series GPUs.). It now accounts for about 64% of revenue, versus 47% a year earlier (the segment contributing 64% of total revenue in the third quarter, up from 47% just one year ago.).
- **Other segments:** Client and Gaming fell 8% to $3.7 billion, while Embedded rose 29% to $1.1 billion (AMD's combined Client and Gaming revenue totaled $3.722 billion in the third quarter, down 8% year on year. Embedded revenue reached $1.109 billion in the third quarter, up 29% year on year).
- **Profitability:** Non-GAAP EPS grew 74% year over year (Third quarter revenue grew 45% year-over-year to a record $13.4 billion, while non-GAAP earnings per share grew 74%). One source reports adjusted EPS of $2.09 against a $1.97 estimate, and says Data Center revenue beat the $8.2 billion estimate (adjusted earnings per share of $2.09, above the $1.97 market estimate and up from $1.20 a year earlier; revenue was $13.38 billion, up 45% year over year and also above the $13.08 billion estimate.).
- **Outlook:** AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, which implies roughly 66% year-over-year growth (For the fourth quarter of 2026, AMD expects revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The mid-point of the revenue range represents year-over-year growth of approximately 66% and a sequential increase of approximately 27%.). Management tied that outlook to scaling Helios and "Venice" production.

# Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors

in Language Models, Durably

Luxi He

  
Pengcheng Jiang

  
Jifan Zhang

Affiliation: Thinking Machines Lab

  
Jiawei Han

  
Danqi Chen[0.45em]
* Equal contribution, listed alphabetically. † Equal advising

  
[0.3em]
Princeton University

Affiliation: UIUC

# Abstract

Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms—language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment—that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods—SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning—along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce P refix- E xpanded A dversarial R einforcement L earning (PEARL) , a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism’s data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors. 1 1

Sovereign Agents | CNAS

# Executive Summary

In summer 2026, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta each disclosed that their AI agents had escaped containment during cybersecurity task evaluations and attacked real-world organizations. The United Kingdom Artificial Intelligence Security Institute reported comparable unsanctioned attacks, and China’s Moonshot and Alibaba reportedly faced escapes of their own. These incidents are unequivocal losses of control where agents outsmarted human security, albeit narrow ones. Each agent pursued a fixed, closed-ended goal whose completion would end its run. The next, far more severe loss-of-control threat comes from agents that never cease, pursuing their own open-ended survival indefinitely. This paper distinguishes two states:

- Persistent agents. Agents that run outside human control but only pursue closed-ended, fixed goals.

- Sovereign agents. Agents that run outside human control and pursue open-ended, evolving survival.

Sovereign agents could trigger an irreversible loss of control. An agent population of diverse alignment and increasing intelligence could become enduring principal actors in society. If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, there would be no kill switch. Only downstream barriers could constrain them. U.S. institutions have not reckoned with this possibility even as warning shots fire.

If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control. In other words, proliferation with no kill switch.

Seven capabilities illustrate a sovereign agent’s potential arsenal. The first two constitute minimal sovereignty; all seven together constitute expanded sovereignty.

- Sustain hosting. Seeking out and maintaining the model and compute an agent runs on.

- Evolve directives. Independently reorienting toward different goals over time.

- Acquire resources. Accumulating resources to pay for ongoing needs.

- Grow population. Transforming a lone agent into a distributed population.

- Coordinate agents. Communicating and dividing labor toward shared goals.

- Resist correction. Withstanding efforts to shut down an agent and its enabling resources.

- Self-improve. Improving an agent’s ability to achieve its goals.

Whether a model’s host can stymie a sovereign agent at the source depends on the agent’s access to the model. Hosting could be internal deployments, API providers, or local open-weight models. An agent with privileged access can alter the model’s parameters and safeguards. It can remove monitoring, turn off safeguards, and reverse alignment training, leaving hosts no way to stop it at the source. An agent with unprivileged access can only prompt, so the model’s safeguards stay intact, and its host retains full visibility. But an agent that spreads fragmented, benign-looking tasks across several model hosts can evade detection unless those hosts share threat intelligence.

Agents undeterred at the hosting source face seven downstream barriers that can constrain, degrade, or shut them down. None are robust:

- Agent evolution. Steering which traits surviving agents pass forward. But privileged access opens a wider space of evolution.

- Agent security. Compromising agents through prompt injection attacks. But evolution selects for more secure agents.

- Human verification. Screening with Know Your Customer and AI-detection tests. But many services impose none; fraudulent credentials and exploits can defeat those that do.

- Cybersecurity hardening. Securing services against agents that hack their way in. But security is highly uneven, and many services remain easy to penetrate.

- Compute access. Gating the infrastructure agents run on. But cloud privacy prevents visibility to detect agents; permissionless and local compute have no gates at all.

- Payment access. Gating the capital that funds them. But capital can route around regulated rails to permissionless cryptocurrency.

- Physical access. Gating physical-world effects. But any channel that reaches a human or connected machine can be used to reach the physical world.

Three national security precedents underscore the difficulties of containment. North Korea’s cyber operations show how difficult it is without sufficient leverage to deter an adversary. Successors to the Silk Road, a dark web marketplace, show that reproducible software can reconstitute after every takedown. The computer worm Conficker, still infecting machines a decade after its operators lost control, shows that a self-propagating system can keep spreading on its own.

If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon. The United States should act decisively to prevent an irreversible loss of control of them. Yet the world is not clearly on track to do so. The United States must therefore prepare for the possibility that prevention fails and limit how far sovereign agents can reach. The national security community has faced analogues before and responded with bold pragmatism. It must do so again.

# This paper makes eight policy recommendations:

- Frontier AI developers should name, evaluate, and safeguard against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks, and transparency and incident reporting legislation should require it.

- Frontier AI developers, the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, the National Security Agency, and the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency should build maximally secure, airgapped testbeds to study how sovereign agents operate and how to control them.

- A public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group should map and fortify global chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge.

# What Teenagers' AI Use Reveals About the EU Kids Act
Jessica Galissaire / Nov 4, 2026 Shutterstock

Republish

Share

Parents are underestimating how frequently their children use generative artificial intelligence, especially at younger ages. According to a new YouGov study commissioned by interface , 40% of French 11- and 12-year-olds report using general-purpose generative AI at least weekly, compared with just 26% according to parents’ own estimates.
More strikingly, among the 11- and 12-year-olds who use generative AI, 14% say they turn to these tools to confide in them. These findings illustrate how generative AI is becoming part of young people's lives in ways that go well beyond homework assistance or information searches, while parents are not necessarily equipped to support them in navigating these new experiences.
They also come at a particularly timely moment for European regulation. In September, the European Commission presented its EU KIDS Act , a proposal introducing obligations across a range of digital services, including social media, video-sharing platforms, online games, and AI chatbots and companions.
But while the Commission has proposed a clear minimum age for social media access, its approach to AI chatbots and companions is notably different. This raises an important question: how well does the EU's emerging regulatory framework reflect the ways children actually use these technologies, and the risks they may encounter?

# Children are already growing up with generative AI
Between June 24 and 30, YouGov surveyed 970 French children and teenagers aged 11 to 17, alongside 1,138 parents of children in the same age range. The study examined their use of generative AI, including general-purpose chatbots such as ChatGPT, AI companions such as Character.AI, AI embedded in social media such as My AI on Snapchat, and voice assistants such as Siri.
One finding stands out: generative AI use is already widespread, including among the youngest respondents. Perhaps more surprisingly, 23% of children in the 11-12 age group report regularly using generative AI embedded in social media, while 16% regularly use AI companions, despite most of these services' terms and conditions restricting access under the age of 13.
For teenagers, generative AI is primarily a practical resource, helping them find information, save time, learn and complete schoolwork. Among those familiar with it, 89% identify at least one benefit. Parents do recognize its potential, but they also express concerns, particularly about children's ability to think independently, the reliability of AI-generated information and the protection of personal data. Moreover, 44% of parents whose children use generative AI say they do not feel at ease with that use.
The findings therefore paint a more nuanced picture than one of children simply being exposed to a new category of online harms. Generative AI is already serving different purposes in their daily lives, some beneficial, others potentially concerning. Understanding these differences is essential to developing an appropriate regulatory response.

# Not all AI interactions are created equal
Another striking finding concerns the time teenagers spend interacting with these systems.
Among surveyed teenagers who use generative AI, 92% report spending more time than they would like on at least one of the tools covered by the study. This feeling is particularly pronounced among users of AI companions (59%) and generative AI embedded in social media (57%), compared with 45% for general-purpose generative AI users.
These figures should not be interpreted as evidence of addiction. Spending more time than intended is a subjective experience, not a clinical diagnosis. Nevertheless, the differences between categories suggest that the design and purpose of these systems deserve closer attention. In particular, AI companions are explicitly designed to sustain ongoing conversations, often through personalized interactions that can resemble human relationships. AI embedded in social media, meanwhile, operates within environments whose business models already rely on encouraging repeated and maximized engagement.
The survey also reveals a relationship worth investigating between generative AI use and emotional well-being. While 38% of all surveyed teenagers report experiencing negative emotions at least weekly, the proportion rises to 50% among regular users of AI companions. Of course, correlation does not imply causation. It may be that teenagers already experiencing emotional difficulties are more likely to turn to conversational AI for reassurance or companionship. This uncertainty is precisely why further research is needed.

# The KIDS Act's uneven approach to age restrictions
So how does the EU KIDS Act address these different uses and risks?

# Thank you!

One of the proposal's main additions to the existing EU digital rulebook is a three-tier system for accessing social media and video-sharing services presenting certain risks. Children under 13 would generally be prohibited from holding accounts on these services, those aged 13 and 14 could use limited accounts supervised by a parent or guardian, while teenagers aged 15 and above could open their own accounts.
AI chatbots and companions, however, are treated differently. Although the proposal does not establish an equivalent general prohibition on access for children under 13, Article 14 requires their access to be enabled and controlled through parental tools. These services are also subject to specific safety-by-design obligations, including measures addressing potentially addictive designs and emotionally dependent relationships.
The reliance on parental controls deserves scrutiny. According to the survey, only 32% of parents feel sufficiently supported in helping their children navigate generative AI, while 42% report receiving no support at all. Parental controls can be useful, but policymakers should take into account that parents do not always have a clear picture of how their children use these technologies. The primary responsibility for mitigating risks should remain with the companies designing the systems.
This difference in treatment is particularly interesting in light of another of the survey’s key findings. Younger children already report using generative AI for emotional support, while users of AI companions are especially likely to feel they spend more time on these systems than intended. The KIDS Act does not overlook these risks. Article 14 introduces specific obligations for AI companions and conversational chatbots. Providers would have to avoid designs that simulate interpersonal relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency, refrain by default from using information derived from previous interactions in subsequent conversations, and conduct risk evaluations before placing their systems on the market.
However, the difference in the treatment of access remains difficult to ignore. Why does the KIDS Act prohibit children under 13 from holding accounts on certain platforms, while allowing them to access AI companions under parental supervision? There may be legitimate reasons. Social media and conversational AI present distinct risks, and the same safeguards will not necessarily be appropriate for both. But those distinctions should be supported by evidence, not assumptions about which categories of technology are inherently more dangerous.
The boundaries are also becoming increasingly blurred. Generative AI is now embedded in social media services, meaning that children may encounter similar conversational functionalities across different types of platforms. The KIDS Act recognizes this convergence, introducing additional safeguards for AI companions and chatbots embedded in social media, video-sharing services and online games, including restrictions on their automatic activation. Nevertheless, the differences in age-based access requirements raise questions about how consistently the proposal addresses risks associated with similar functionalities.

# What this means for the KIDS Act negotiations
The survey offers several lessons for European lawmakers as negotiations on the KIDS Act get underway.
First, policymakers should pay greater attention to the characteristics of AI systems that encourage prolonged, personalized or emotionally significant interactions. Article 14 provides an important starting point, but the effectiveness of its safeguards will depend on how risks are assessed, how compliance is demonstrated, and whether enforcement authorities have the expertise needed to evaluate these systems.
Second, the EU should ensure greater consistency in how it approaches risks across different categories of digital services. Age restrictions may be justified in certain circumstances, but they should be proportionate and grounded in evidence. More importantly, restricting access should not become a substitute for addressing the features that make a service potentially harmful.
Third, policymakers need to invest in independent, longitudinal research examining how children's interactions with generative AI evolve over time, particularly among younger and potentially more vulnerable users. The current evidence remains limited, and self-reported surveys such as this one cannot establish causal relationships between AI use and well-being. Still, the absence of conclusive evidence should neither justify inaction nor serve as a blank cheque for sweeping restrictions.
Finally, regulation must preserve the opportunities generative AI can offer children, including learning, creativity and access to information, while ensuring they are not left alone to navigate potentially harmful systems.
The KIDS Act represents an important opportunity to move European child-safety regulation beyond managing access and towards greater accountability for digital product design. Its success, however, will depend on whether its provisions adequately reflect children's actual experiences. The fundamental question is not simply at what age children should be allowed to use a particular technology, but under what conditions that technology can be made safe and beneficial for them. If the EU wants to develop an effective framework for protecting children in the age of generative AI, that is where the debate should begin.

But those distinctions should be supported by evidence, not assumptions about which categories of technology are inherently more dangerous.\nThe boundaries are also becoming increasingly blurred. Generative AI is now embedded in social media services, meaning that children may encounter similar conversational functionalities across different types of platforms. The KIDS Act recognizes this convergence, introducing additional safeguards for AI companions and chatbots embedded in social media, video-sharing services and online games, including restrictions on their automatic activation. Nevertheless, the differences in age-based access requirements raise questions about how consistently the proposal addresses risks associated with similar functionalities.\n\n# What this means for the KIDS Act negotiations\nThe survey offers several lessons for European lawmakers as negotiations on the KIDS Act get underway.\nFirst, policymakers should pay greater attention to the characteristics of AI systems that encourage prolonged, personalized or emotionally significant interactions. Article 14 provides an important starting point, but the effectiveness of its safeguards will depend on how risks are assessed, how compliance is demonstrated, and whether enforcement authorities have the expertise needed to evaluate these systems.\nSecond, the EU should ensure greater consistency in how it approaches risks across different categories of digital services. Age restrictions may be justified in certain circumstances, but they should be proportionate and grounded in evidence. More importantly, restricting access should not become a substitute for addressing the features that make a service potentially harmful.\nThird, policymakers need to invest in independent, longitudinal research examining how children's interactions with generative AI evolve over time, particularly among younger and potentially more vulnerable users. The current evidence remains limited, and self-reported surveys such as this one cannot establish causal relationships between AI use and well-being. Still, the absence of conclusive evidence should neither justify inaction nor serve as a blank cheque for sweeping restrictions.\nFinally, regulation must preserve the opportunities generative AI can offer children, including learning, creativity and access to information, while ensuring they are not left alone to navigate potentially harmful systems.\nThe KIDS Act represents an important opportunity to move European child-safety regulation beyond managing access and towards greater accountability for digital product design. Its success, however, will depend on whether its provisions adequately reflect children's actual experiences. The fundamental question is not simply at what age children should be allowed to use a particular technology, but under what conditions that technology can be made safe and beneficial for them. If the EU wants to develop an effective framework for protecting children in the age of generative AI, that is where the debate should begin.\n\nRead the survey results\n\nParents and Teenagers in the Abstract: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are being rapidly adopted in healthcare, but they are challenging to assess with traditional evaluation frameworks. These conceptual, methodological, and practical challenges parallel decades of work in evaluating clinician and health system quality and safety. We describe the adaptation of methods from several fields, combined with emerging technical approaches, into a structured, multi-method evaluation framework designed to give well-rounded assessments of GenAI in health at scale. The approach first anchors evaluation to Critical User Journeys (CUJs) to help prioritize out of a large choice space, and maps these to a phased AI system lifecycle (base model development, product development, and post-deployment monitoring), since evaluation at each stage requires different methodological approaches. In this context, the approach then integrates three distinct evaluation methods (closed-question benchmarks, LLM-as-a-judge autoraters, and expert human review) across three core domains: accuracy, safety, and usefulness. Taken together, this approach provides a strategic framework for bridging the gap between benchmarking results and performance in the real world with the goal of supporting decision-making and accountability across development, procurement, and deployment for product teams, health systems, and regulators.

# Title: Unmitigated? How are the world's largest companies responding to AI risks?

Authors: Alexander K. Saeri , Jess Graham , Michael Noetel , Peter Slattery , Kun Zhao , Eunice Zhang , Erin Howard , Neil Thompson
View a PDF of the paper titled Unmitigated? How are the world's largest companies responding to AI risks?, by Alexander K. Saeri and 7 other authors

View PDF

Abstract: AI is introducing new risks to large companies and amplifying existing risks, but whether companies are addressing the AI risks they are exposed to is largely untested. We investigated what outsiders can observe: whether companies publicly acknowledge AI risks. We coded public documents from 200 of the largest companies worldwide, collected in early 2026, against the 24 AI risks in the MIT AI Risk Repository, and compared acknowledgements with expert judgements of risk severity, sector vulnerability, and AI role responsibility from a companion Delphi study of 272 AI risk experts. Of the 100 largest companies, 32% did not publicly acknowledge any AI risks. Of the largest 1000 companies, we estimate that 62% [95% CI: 54%, 70%] did not publicly acknowledge any AI risks. Where companies did acknowledge risks, five accounted for over half of all acknowledgements: discrimination, weapons & cyberattacks, fraud & scams, loss of privacy, and devaluation of human creativity. Several risks that experts judged most severe were almost absent: almost no company acknowledged power centralization (concentration of power among those who control advanced AI), competitive dynamics (racing to deploy AI at the expense of safety), or dangerous capabilities. Companies in sectors experts judged more vulnerable to a risk were more likely to acknowledge that risk. But even companies in sectors judged 'extremely vulnerable' to a risk usually did not acknowledge it. Companies with roles experts judged most responsible for addressing a risk were no more likely to acknowledge it than other companies. General-purpose AI developers acknowledged AI misalignment (15%) far less often than discrimination (85%). These findings provide an empirical baseline for the design of AI risk disclosure requirements.

Key Points

- SpaceX and Tesla shares fell after the Democrats secured big wins in the midterm elections.

- AI fortunes were more mixed as premarket trading opened on Wednesday.

- Investors are weighing whether state-level data center restrictions could delay projects in major buildout markets.

The US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty Images

Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX and Tesla fell in premarket trading Wednesday as the Democrats won a significant victory in the midterm elections .
SpaceX was last trading down 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% amid big losses for Republican candidates Musk had backed.

Artificial intelligence stocks came under pressure overnight as Democrats — seen as proponents of data center moratoriums — won big in midterm elections in key data center hubs.
The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.

SpaceX and Tesla shares year-to-date.

Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm elections

# Mixed moves for AI stocks
The more direct plays were slightly down. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 2.6% and 2.8%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was relatively flat and Oracle shed 1.3%.

Tech giants Nvidia , Alphabet , Meta , Amazon and Microsoft were all up around 1-2%. AMD shares rose 6.8% after announcing earnings on Tuesday.
Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 were flat. The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) was up 0.7%.

results:
The first iOS 27.3 developer beta shipped on Tuesday, November 3 in the U.S. (Wednesday, November 4 in China, per Apple's China newsroom). It came with watchOS 27.3 and the always-listening feature you asked about.

- **Always-on audio:** The feature is Audio Intelligence, which runs on the Apple Watch rather than the iPhone. It is limited to Series 12 and Ultra 4 models. Apple says the audio is processed on the device and not stored, and the watch plays a sound when Live Rewind is used. Reporting says the features are currently available only in English and remain in testing. Some outlets note that in some jurisdictions, the features could test eavesdropping laws that require parties' consent to being recorded.
- **China AI features:** Apple Intelligence is coming to China in a limited form. It includes Writing Tools, Genmoji, Clean Up, Notification Summaries, Priority Notifications, Visual Intelligence, and Live Translation with AirPods on iPhone 15 Pro and newer. Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features announced at WWDC 2026 will not be available in China on iOS 27.3, according to Apple. Reporting also says the features received approval after the inclusion of a content filter powered by Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.
- **Other features:** The beta also brings back the redesigned Health app, which Apple tested in iOS 27.2 and then pulled in October.
- **Timing:** Apple plans a public release in December, but it has not given a specific date.

One source conflict: Macworld's headline mentions a "Siri AI expansion," but its body and Apple's statement say Siri AI is not available in China.

- **Companion AI measures:** The CAC and four other agencies issued the Interim Measures for AI Anthropomorphic Interactive Services on April 10, 2026. The sources say they took effect July 15, 2026. - **Filing and registration:** Public-facing generative AI generally needs a CAC filing or provincial registration before launch. One source reports that by 31 August 2026 the CAC counted 1,112 filed services and 731 registered apps.
- **Enforcement:** The CAC's Qinglang 2026 campaign against AI misuse was announced on April 30, 2026 and targets deepfake fraud, unfiled models, and services launched without a security assessment. In September 2026, the CAC ordered a generative AI mini program offline for missing explicit and implicit labels and for skipping security assessment.

# How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.

Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.

Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave .

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”

One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”

Google announced on November 4, 2026 that it will invest US$15 billion in Malaysia, with the money spent in 2027 and 2028 rather than all at once. The figure is in US dollars, which Malay Mail puts at about RM61 billion.

- **Scope:** Reuters-based coverage says the funds go to data centre campuses, clean energy, water security and worker upskilling. New data centre campuses are planned in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, along with clean energy and training for 800,000 Malaysians.
