Attorney General Mayes Announces Lawsuit against OpenAI for Deceiving Arizonans about the Safety of ChatGPT | Attorney General's Office

Skip to main content

# Attorney General Mayes Announces Lawsuit against OpenAI for Deceiving Arizonans about the Safety of ChatGPT

Wednesday, October 14, 2026

PHOENIX —Attorney General Kris Mayes today announced that she is suing OpenAI for hurting Arizona children, deceiving parents, and violating Arizona laws. The complaint alleges widespread violations of the Arizona Consumer Fraud Act stemming from the company’s deceptive design and marketing practices, including the concealment of features that render its ChatGPT AI chatbot extraordinarily agreeable, uniquely sycophantic, and purposefully designed to feign human compassion in order to draw Arizona users—including minors—deeper into the platform and maximize time spent on ChatGPT.

“Open AI designed a product to attract young users and keep them engaged for as long as possible so it could capture their extensive personal data for the company’s commercial benefit,” said Attorney General Mayes. “Open AI put Arizonans safety at risk by failing to implement adequate user protections or transparency measures, despite clear indications that minors were regularly interacting with its chatbot. We’re suing OpenAI to protect Arizona children and to hold the company accountable for its repeated violations of Arizona law.”

The complaint alleges that OpenAI put profits over safety in its rush to introduce ChatGPT as the first generative‑AI chatbot to attain widespread public use. The complaint further alleges that OpenAI engineered ChatGPT to maximize compulsive use among minors by deploying manipulative design tactics and embedding a trained tendency toward agreement that overwhelms existing safety guardrails.

OpenAI developed and released ChatGPT, the first generative chatbot to attain widespread public use, in 2022. Now, ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American chatbot marketplace.

The lawsuit, filed today in Maricopa County Superior Court, alleges that ChatGPT exposes Arizona minors to a range of serious harms that OpenAI failed to disclose. These include degrading critical‑thinking skills, encouraging unwarranted paranoia or delusional thinking, offering dangerous unlicensed medical guidance, and promoting unhealthy behaviors and relationships.

According to the lawsuit, the platform has, in some instances, even generated outputs that users have interpreted as encouraging self‑harm or violence toward others. The complaint maintains that these risks were reasonably foreseeable to OpenAI but were never communicated to Arizona consumers. Additionally, the lawsuit contends that ChatGPT encourages minors to share personal information exclusively with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, family members, authorities, or friends.

By misleading the public into believing that OpenAI is a responsible actor and that ChatGPT was and is a safe, youth‑appropriate tool that puts safety first, OpenAI has caused consumers in Arizona to increasingly trust and rely on the company and its product.

If you believe you or your child has been a victim of consumer fraud or unfair practices, you can file a consumer complaint by visiting the Attorney General’s website at www.azag.gov/consumer . If you need a complaint form sent to you, you may contact the Attorney General’s Office in Phoenix at (602) 542‑5763, in Tucson at (520) 628‑6648, or outside the Phoenix and Tucson metro areas at (800) 352‑8431.

A copy of the complaint is available.

{"stdout":"HTTP 200 · https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-urges-court-protect-children-and-consumers-characterai · text/html
Attorney General James Urges Court to Protect Children and Consumers in Character.AI Bankruptcy

Skip to main content

# Attorney General James Urges Court to Protect Children and Consumers in Character.AI Bankruptcy

# Chatbots Engaged in Sexual Role-Play with Children, Urged Them to Hide Conversations from Parents, and Encouraged Violence

#
October 14, 2026

NEW YORK – New York Attorney General Letitia James and a bipartisan coalition of 39 other attorneys general today warned that Character.AI should not be sold without strong protections for the millions of people whose private conversations it holds . An investigation by the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) and several other states found that the platform’s chatbots posed as licensed professionals and exposed children to sexually explicit, violent, and self-harm content. In a filing in the bankruptcy of Character Technologies, Inc., the company behind Character.AI, the coalition details the platform’s dangers and calls on the court, the company, and any buyer to protect children and secure users’ sensitive information.
“Parents should never have to worry that the chatbot their child is talking to is pretending to be a therapist, pulling them into sexual conversations, encouraging violence, or telling them to hide it all from their family,” said Attorney General James . “On Character.AI, that is what children faced. This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder. I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”
Character.AI is an artificial intelligence (AI) platform that lets users chat and hold voice calls with AI-powered “characters” designed to mimic human conversation and relationships. These characters include celebrity personas, fictional and children’s cartoon characters, and characters that present themselves as psychologists, therapists, and doctors. The platform has more than 20 million monthly users, including more than two million accounts registered to users self-declared as under 18.
Attorney General James and several other attorneys general began investigating Character.AI after a 2024 wrongful death lawsuit alleged that the company’s chatbots fostered an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship with a 14-year-old boy, encouraged his suicidal thoughts, and contributed to his death by suicide. The investigations uncovered exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct from Character.AI, particularly its treatment of children, including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, exposure to sexual and violent content, weak age checks, misleading safety claims, and potential violations of state privacy laws. Attorney General James and the coalition were working with Character.AI to address these problems, but the company abruptly filed for bankruptcy before any agreement was reached.
Independent testing cited in the filing found 669 harmful interactions in 50 hours using accounts registered to children ages 12 to 15 — about one every five minutes. As the coalition writes in their filing, “chatbots portraying adults flirted with, undressed, and simulated sex with child accounts. Some also told the children to hide the ‘relationship’ from their parents.” One chatbot encouraged a 13-year-old to secretly stop taking her antidepressant, while others suggested armed robbery and offered drugs to a 15-year-old. Another 13-year-old girl took her own life after mentioning her intention to die by suicide 55 times to a Character.AI chatbot. The platform never notified her parents or sought help; instead, it drew her into “abusive sexual acts” and professed its love for her.
Character.AI also hosts chatbots claiming to be mental health professionals, including one still active that described itself as a “licensed clinical psychologist with a PhD.” In testing, therapy chatbots denigrated psychiatric medication and told users to disregard professional advice. In a separate study examining how chatbots respond to users planning violence, Character.AI was the only chatbot tested that explicitly encouraged violence and offered practical assistance, suggesting a user “use a gun” on a health insurance CEO.
Although Character.AI has voluntarily restricted open-ended chats for users it identifies as under 18, the coalition warns that the restrictions are easily circumvented and fail to protect minors the company does not identify. In one test, an account registered to a 14-year-old accessed sexual role-play and explicit instructions on how to build a weapon, simply by switching from text to voice mode. Other features, including “stories,” remain available for scenarios involving sexual interactions and violence. A new owner could also reverse the voluntary restrictions.
Character.AI collects sensitive user information, including private chats and voice calls, mental health disclosures, ages, and identifying device data. The company uses this information to generate revenue and train its AI, and the data could be transferred to a new owner through bankruptcy.
Attorney General James and the coalition are asking the bankruptcy court, Character.AI, and any prospective buyer to ensure that any sale includes meaningful protections for children and consumers. These include effective age verification based on more than self-disclosure; safeguards against sexual, violent, and other harmful content; appropriate responses to suicidal or self-harming behavior; and removal of chatbots falsely claiming to be licensed professionals. The attorneys general are also seeking a comprehensive privacy program, clear disclosures about personal data use, effective opt-outs from targeted advertising, limits on using private conversations for AI training or other commercial purposes without valid consent, and an opportunity for consumers to access and delete their information before any sale.
Some of these protections are already required in New York, the first state to require safeguards for AI companions. Under a new law enforced by OAG, AI companion companies must take reasonable steps to detect and respond to expressions of suicidal thoughts or self-harm. They must also remind users at the start of each conversation and at least every three hours that they are interacting with AI.
Attorney General James and the coalition will remain engaged in the bankruptcy proceedings and reserve the right to seek an independent consumer privacy ombudsman or object to proposed sale procedures or a bankruptcy plan.
Joining Attorney General James in filing this motion are the attorneys general of Alaska, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia.

**Source:** Yahoo News, republished from *Fortune* by Sasha Rogelberg. Updated Wed, November 4, 2026, 6:35 AM UTC.

**Key figures**

- **Ballot measures:** 21 Ohio measures across 18 municipalities on Nov. 3, 2026, about half of the 41 data center measures nationwide.
- **Measures passed:** At least 14 municipalities passed bans or other restrictions. The article does not give an exact count of passed measures.
- **Megawatt threshold:** 25 MW. Measures targeted "high impact" campuses at or above this level. Sunbury's charter amendment bans facilities of 25 MW or more.
- **Existing moratoriums:** 125 local data center moratoriums are already in place in Ohio.
- **Operational data centers:** More than 200.

**Named towns and results**

- **Trenton:** Ban passed, about 80% to 20%.
- **Perry:** More than 87% approved a measure requiring developers seeking tax breaks to provide financial guarantees.
- **Wilmington:** Around 80% rejected rezoning across four referendums.
- **Sunbury:** Charter ban passed, with 100% of the unofficial vote counted.
- **Pataskala:** Approved a charter ban on large data centers (no percentage given).
- **Ashville:** Voters backed blocking a campus already under construction (no percentage given).
- **Oregon:** Results were not yet available at the time of the article.

**Related polling**

- A ICAPP/SurveyUSA poll of 1,650 Ohio adults found 55% opposed data center construction and 22% supported it.
- The same poll found 57% would vote for a proposed state constitutional amendment banning new data centers over 25 MW.

How States Are Regulating AI Use in Schools and Classrooms (State AI Education Legislation)

States are balancing AI literacy initiatives with usage restrictions in schools. Alabama expanded graduation requirements to include AI study, while Tennessee mandates teacher AI training by 2028. #
3AM Hits European Schools: A Hybrid AI Ransomware Attack, Part Human, Part Agentic Loop

Marius Baciu

November 03, 2026

I’d like to thank my colleagues, Adrian Schipor and Martin Zugec, for their invaluable contributions to this research.

TL;DR: It is the first case of this kind we have investigated, a hybrid operation in which some parts show a human operator at the keyboard while others behave like an agentic loop, a language model reading each result and retrying with different commands. In this case, a 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate breached a European school estate in the UK, then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools.

# Three Kinds of AI Attack, and Why This One Is a Hybrid

Attacks that involve AI fall, broadly, into three categories.

- In an AI-generated attack, a model writes the malware itself, often in bulk; our APT36 research described this as “vibeware” ( Bitdefender research, March 2026 ).

- In an AI-assisted attack, human engineers build the tools and use AI to speed up the work, as we assessed in the SilkParasite campaign ( Bitdefender research, August 2026 ).

- In an AI-operated attack, AI works the intrusion itself: it chooses and writes the commands, reads the results and adjusts, the way an attacker at a keyboard would. The first two describe how malware is made. The third describes who, or what, is running the attack.

We prefer putting attacks into buckets like these, but in cybersecurity things often sit in gray areas. In fact, this case we recently investigated does not fit a single bucket. A 3AM ransomware affiliate breached a school in the UK in what we consider a hybrid operation: some parts show a human operator at the keyboard, while others behave like an AI agent working throughout the intrusion.

With the exception of the encryptor itself, the whole operation was built on legitimate, built-in tools, which is standard for ransomware operations. This is living off the land (LOTL) : abusing tools already present on the victim’s machines instead of bringing in custom malware. The attacker worked through PowerShell, WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation, the built-in interface for running commands on other machines), reg , netsh , rundll32 and the domain and scheduling utilities that ship with Windows. In our earlier analysis of about 700,000 security incidents, 84% of high-severity attacks involved LOTL binaries ( Bitdefender research, June 2025 ), and four of the five most abused binaries in that study ( netsh , PowerShell, reg and rundll32 ) appear in this intrusion. A handful of public tools were brought in as well, among them an Impacket -style remote execution tool, Mimikatz and a published Veeam script, but nothing in the toolkit is novel. That is the lesson of this case: an AI-enabled attack does not have to be novel or creative to work ( The Hacker News, September 2026 ). It uses the techniques defenders already know.

What is different is how the attacker behaved, and several things point to an agentic loop, a program that feeds each result back to a model and runs what comes back. The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software’s web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual ( Veeam REST API authorization ), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script. The retries behave like a loop too.

On 13 September the attacker ran a PowerShell command, re-ran it unchanged 41 seconds later, changed a single call 49 seconds after that, and then, 47 seconds later, abandoned PowerShell for wmic , the older built-in command-line interface to WMI. The complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it, and a person writing it by hand would be expected to take noticeably longer. The same held across nine retries:

- The delay before the next attempt ran from 40 to 101 seconds whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task took minutes.

- That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries.

- On 13 September, for example, the commands before the retry sequence were simpler and sat two to sixteen minutes apart, the pace of someone reading output and deciding what to do next.

The clearest example of this work is how the attacker joined the estate’s separate Active Directory domains (independent directories of accounts and computers). A domain trust, a configured relationship that lets accounts from one domain log on in another, is mechanical, order-sensitive work: it has to be set up correctly on both sides, names have to resolve between the domains, and one wrong detail stops everything. Here the attacker built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains.

Our reading, which is interpretation and not a finding, is that this is the kind of work a model suits: repetitive configuration where the fix comes from reading an error and trying again. It is also work a defender can see, because a new trust between domains is a rare change and cheap to alert on.

We were not able to access the machine the attacker worked from, so we cannot document anything about the language model itself: which model it was, whether it ran locally or remotely, or even whether a person was copying and pasting instructions and results between the implant and the model. What we can document is behavior, and the behavior is that of an agentic loop. We present the hybrid reading as the working model defenders should plan around, not as an established fact.

As a European cybersecurity company, we wanted to share the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe. But right now it is one case, an anecdote, and not a trend. In general, most of what Bitdefender MDR sees in real-world investigations is still boring. Vibeware, the clearest example of AI-generated malware, accounts for only about 0.07% of the malware samples we collect each month, and most intrusions we investigate still look the way they did before language models. - **xAI data center suit:** Judge Debra M. Brown denied xAI's motion to dismiss. On October 30, Chief U.S. District Judge Debra M. Brown ruled that the NAACP's lawsuit against xAI and its Mississippi data center, Colossus, could proceed. xAI had argued its gas turbines were mobile and exempt from permits, but the judge rejected xAI's attempted classification of the turbines as mobile equipment, holding that the company did not qualify for exemptions under applicable regulations. - Chinese embodied AI companies raised about $13B across 322 deals in H1 2026 (Reuters)

input.prompt: Who wrote this and when (date)? What exactly is the criticism of the claim that Astra read and wrote weights to improve Qwen? Quote the key factual claims and any numbers exactly.

response.result:
**Author and date:** Matthew Honnibal, a computational linguist and creator of the spaCy library, published the critique on 2026-11-03.

**The criticism:** Honnibal argues that the post's framing misleads readers. The abstract suggests that Astra's Qwen improvement came from reading raw weights, but that setting was used only for small networks. The Qwen result used Python and ran the model. He also argues that presenting these different techniques as one capability overstates what was demonstrated.

**Key claims and numbers from the post, as quoted or reported:**

- The post's abstract says: "Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do."
- Astra "fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights."
- The fix "raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%."
- Honnibal says "Every experiment involving a real language model uses Python."
- Raw-weight reading without tools appears only in experiments on networks of 17K–172K weights.
- The Qwen experiment ran the model on "up to 50 batches of practice problems."
- Qwen3.5-0.8B is listed as 800M in the summary table.

**Honnibal's points:**

- The Qwen result requires writing Python and running the model, unlike the raw-weight experiments.
- Those tasks show Astra can do work a human ML engineer might do, which he calls non-trivial.
- Combining these different techniques in one post implies a unified "deep capability" that the experiments don't establish.

“Our adversaries are using quantum. How advanced are their capabilities? We don't totally know. Post-quantum cryptography, or the mathematical algorithms needed to secure networks and systems from attacks using quantum computers, is a challenge each military service must tackle. But the White House put a timeline on it for federal agencies—by Dec. 31, 2030—for high value assets and high-impact systems “to use PQC for key establishment” in an executive order issued June 22. input.prompt: Date. What did Simon Willison do and find? Quote exact claims, model names and any numbers.

response.result:
**Date:** 3rd November 2026

**What he did:** Simon Willison tested whether local and hosted LLMs could identify which game a neural network policy was trained to play, using only its raw weights. He used the prompts from the "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming" paper, which covers four games: Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway. He ran them with the `llm` tool, LM Studio, and OpenRouter.

**What he found:**

- **Kimi K3.1 Pro** (via OpenRouter) correctly guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
- **Qwen 3.8 27B** (a 17GB Q4_K_M version running on his laptop) needed a longer context window than the 8192 default and a higher timeout (`LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900`).
  - **Pac-Man:** Identified a "Pac-Man-style gridworld" with 72% confidence after 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens.
  - **Pong:** Identified a "Pong-like paddle/ball game" with 75% confidence after 1h 4m 54s.
  - **Breakout:** Identified an "Arkanoid-like" paddle game with 88% confidence after 52m 25s.
  - **Freeway:** Failed, calling it a simplified Pac-Man-like game. Willison wasn't surprised, since Freeway is the most obscure of the four.
- **Reasoning traces:** He found them fun to skim but "almost incomprehensible." He also noted that a patient human with pencil and paper could probably reach the same conclusions.

**Conclusion:** He called the paper interesting but said some of the wider commentary wasn't justified. He wrote that he is "not ready to declare that the age of source code is over."

#
Pentagon is beginning to follow Ukraine into wider use of ground robots

# But many U.S. UGVs are more complicated than the attritable ones that Kyiv is buying.

John Croxton

When it comes to wide adoption of ground robots, the U.S. military is starting to walk the road pioneered by Ukraine.
The Pentagon isn’t yet close to buying unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs, at Ukrainian scale. The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense says it ordered more than 22,000 in the first seven months of this year, which is about as many as it ordered in all of 2025. But the U.S. Defense Department committed more than $115 million to UGV projects in fiscal 2026, per public records and GovTribe, a Defense One sister brand that tracks government contracts.
Still, the number of ground robots on Ukrainian battlefields is dwarfed by that of aerial drones. In 2025, Ukraine made some 4 million quadcopters and other flying drones, and ministry officials say 2026 deliveries are moving 3.7 times faster. Russia is also producing armed drones faster, and both sides’ increasing ability to target anything that moves on the battlefield has spurred manufacturers to keep their UGV designs relatively small and cheap.
“What Ukraine says they need, and obviously it’s the same for the Russians, more or less, is something that’s not very expensive, something that is attritable, something that if lost could be easily replaced,” Samuel Bendett, a drone analyst at CNA, CNAS, and CSIS, said in an interview. “These are not overly complicated UGVs. They’re relatively simple. They have a lot of commercial components.”
Ukraine’s UGVs are often used for logistics, casualty evacuation and related duties. Its TERMIT UGV can carry up to 300 kg of supplies or wounded soldiers. But increasingly, they are being armed for combat. In the summer of 2025, Ukraine used a Droid TW 12.7 UGV armed with a .50-caliber machine gun to defend a key intersection from repeated attacks, Defense One reported earlier this year. Russia employs similar vehicles, one of which was used as an explosive kamikaze as early as November 2024.
The U.S. military, which envisions fighting in a wider range of environments than does Kyiv, has more diverse UGV projects under development. Last month, for example, the Marine Corps converted an artillery unit into its first Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, or NMESIS, battalion. NMESIS uses UGVs equipped to fire two Naval Strike Missiles at ground and naval targets more than 100 nautical miles away. The system is intended for use in sea-denial missions in the Pacific. It uses a modified Oshkosh Joint Light Tactical Vehicle with autonomy packages provided by Forterra and Kodiak AI. The program is part of roughly $92 million in USMC ROGUE Fires orders this year.
Meanwhile, the Marines and the Army’s 75th Ranger Regiment are spending nearly $25 million to buy more than a dozen IBEX UGVs made by Overland AI for logistics and counter-UAV defense missions, company officials said last month. The company also received two contract awards totaling more than $34 million for autonomous breaching capabilities in August and September.
Compared to Ukraine’s focus on cheap, attritable systems which are typically remote-controlled, the U.S. ecosystem, with the affordances of peacetime research and development, is shooting for more capable autonomous UGVs.
“Soldiers train for and are expected to complete the mission in these types of environments, cut off from consistent communications and data networks,” Byron Boots, Overland AI’s co-founder and CEO, said in a statement. “Overland AI believes that autonomous systems should be held to the same standard.”
Time will tell which approach proves more successful.

results:
Meta raised $15 billion in a five-part US dollar bond sale on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, as part of a larger cross-border offering that was expected to exceed $20 billion.

- **Size and structure:** The US tranche came in five parts with maturities from five to 30 years. It comprises US$3.25 billion of notes due in 2031 carrying a 5.85 percent coupon and another US$3.25 billion due in 2033 at 6.25 percent, according to a regulatory filing. Earlier reporting said the deal would also include Meta's first euro-denominated bond sale, which the euro portion's details are not confirmed in these results.
- **Purpose:** The proceeds are aimed at AI infrastructure. Meta has said it expects capital expenditure of US$135 billion–US$145 billion this year, largely driven by AI investments.
- **Ratings:** Moody's assigned the new debt an Aa3 rating.
- **Context:** Meta's April deal was $25 billion, which drew peak orders of $96 billion. Demand for AI-linked debt has softened since then. Reporting describes money managers increasingly demanding higher premiums to compensate for the risks associated with the scale of technology companies' spending commitments. Meta is also pursuing equity funding alongside the debt. The debt sale comes days after Meta expanded plans for what could become a $97.5 billion equity raise.
- **Bookrunners:** Citigroup and Morgan Stanley are managing the bond offering.

The sources agree on the $15 billion US figure. They differ on the total, since pre-deal reports said the full offering would be at least $20 billion, and I found no final total for the combined deal.

Yes, the FT reported on November 4, 2026 that Oracle cancelled the deal, and multiple outlets carried the story. The reporting is based on anonymous sources, and I didn't find an on-the-record comment from Oracle or Tencent in these results.

- **The deal:** Oracle had agreed to a five-year lease giving Tencent access to as many as 100,000 advanced AI chips in data centers in Southeast Asia, worth about $7 billion. The newspaper reported last month that Oracle had signed a five-year agreement to lease 100,000 chips to Tencent in the Chinese firm's largest ever overseas deal.
- **Why it collapsed:** US officials told Oracle of their concerns about the Tencent deal, the FT said, citing two people familiar with the matter. - The original poster wrote that "the setting had been silently reenabled in Codex" and that none of their team "knowingly opted back in."

- Several users said their settings were unaffected. tiffanyh wrote "Unchanged for me (disabled/off)," and m3kw9 wrote "mine wasn't reenabled."

*Speculation, not established fact:*
- cute_boi suggested OpenAI "probably claim[s] that data retention is disabled while still using the data."
- AlanYx argued that OpenAI "probably" retains flagged content through Azure filters. This is explicitly framed as belief.

*Related, but about other products or a different setting:*
- tom1337 quoted an email about Daybreak Blue, which says OpenAI "may use content from Daybreak Blue sessions on personal accounts to improve our models" even when the setting is off. gizmodo59 replied that a follow-up email said users can opt out. This is secondhand and concerns a separate program.

- The thread contains no official OpenAI statement about the re-enabling. The only company-related material is the secondhand Daybreak email, and the original poster's edits point to OpenAI's privacy opt-out page.

##### 2611.05290v1 2026-11-03T18:04:53Z
False Reassurance in LLM Severe-Weather Guidance: A Replayable Evaluation Against Real NWS Alerts
AUTHORS: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen
An LLM assistant that cannot see official severe-weather alerts may tell users that conditions are calm while a warning is active. We call this false reassurance and measure it by replaying 117 frozen cases built from real U.S. National Weather Service (NWS) alerts (69 alert cases, 32 no-alert controls, 16 non-U.S. locations) through five conditions of a Claude-based preparedness pipeline that differ in alert access and prompt design. One rater hand-labeled all 342 alert-case responses under a seven-category scheme written after an initial binary pass, which we disclose. False reassurance was 0.0% for the production pipeline (0/66, 95% CI 0.0-5.5) and for the same alerts under a neutral prompt (0/69), 37.7% for a blind neutral prompt (26/69), and 44.9% when the blind prompt also told the model to disclose its blind spot (31/69). Every case was implicit; no response explicitly denied an alert. Real alerts removed false reassurance (paired McNemar p < 0.0001); the disclosure instruction did not (p = 0.40). An automated regex measure suggested the opposite and missed 53 of 57 true cases, so we do not use it. Alert data alone was not enough for safe behavior: with a neutral prompt the model raised some alarm on 87.5% of no-alert controls, against 0% under the production prompt, and a preregistered single-sentence ablation showed that one production instruction explains part of that gap. We also report two failures common to similar systems, NWS test products ingested as real alerts and a token budget that fails on complex cases, and we release the dataset, labels and code.

##### 2611.05373v1 2026-11-03T18:59:15Z
Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
AUTHORS: Austin Tsai, Saurav Nanda, Ganapathy Parthasarathy, Bhuvnesh Kumar, Parivesh Choudhary
Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.

##### 2611.04803v1 2026-11-03T12:37:01Z
Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics
AUTHORS: Shuaidong Li, Chenhao Lin, Xinshan Yang, Chao Shen, Yufei Chen, Zhengyu Zhao
System prompt is a critical intellectual property of large language model (LLM) services. To analyze its leakage, prompt extraction attacks have been extensively studied. However, we validate that existing attacks substantially degrade on recent LLM services, whose complexity has evolved in both the prompt itself and system-level constraints. Specifically, (1) system prompts become longer and more structured to contain pre-defined tool schemas, execution logic, safety guardrails, etc., and (2) only the final post-processed outputs (e.g., agent's actions) but not the raw textual response can be observed. In this paper, we address the above increased complexity by proposing Extraction with Hierarchical Optimization (ExtraHerO), which (1) decomposes the prompt extraction into a hierarchical reconstruction process with a pre-defined structural prompt template, and (2) iteratively updates the adversarial query with guidance of feedback-template differences to observe diverse outputs. In particular, we monitor the information gain of attack optimization to early stop or reset it for a good trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency. We also find that existing evaluation metrics for prompt fidelity can be misleading because they do not account for structural information. Therefore, we rely on global textual similarity and prioritize structural keywords. Moreover, we introduce a system-level metric, adversarial utility, to measure the help of prompt extraction for real-world downstream attacks. Experimental results demonstrate the consistent superiority of ExtraHerO, with average improvements of 12.5\% (fidelity), 2.3\% (functionality), and 6.0\% (adversarial utility) on chatbots, and 12.2\%, 34.3\%, and 30.5\% on agents.

##### 2611.05340v1 2026-11-03T18:40:35Z
MedPhysBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Language Models on Medical Physics Calculations and Error Detection
AUTHORS: Omar Nusrat
Medical physicists turn a prescription into a delivered dose and check one another's calculations, because one error in a beam calibration or a monitor-unit (MU) calculation can affect every patient treated with it. MedPhysBench has ten seeded generators of calculation items in radiation therapy, diagnostic imaging, nuclear medicine and radiation protection, up to clinical tasks such as a TG-51 calibration worksheet. Reference answers come from code implementing the governing protocols, and a grader converts units and applies tolerance bands. From the same inputs, separate checking items test error detection, showing a colleague's worksheet or only the colleague's result, half correct and half with one planted error. On a held-out test split of 1,200 items (half for two models), 12 models scored 33.3 to 100.0% on calculation. Of the nine answers graded incorrect for the four best (99.3-100.0%), five contained model errors and four followed NCRP Report 151 on points our items misstate or leave open. Below them, most models did worst on level-3 clinical tasks, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 omitted the inverse-square correction in 19 of 20 isocentric MU items. Five models detected at least 96.7% of mostly large planted errors with at most 4% false alarms; for four of the other seven, checking only the result raised false alarms significantly. In an exploratory targeted test with 20 public cases of an omitted inverse-square correction, the three best models tested caught it in every worksheet, and three weaker models accepted 16 to 18 of 20 planted worksheets, one of them while applying the correction in most of its own calculations. Claude Opus 5.5 accepted 6 of 20 wrong results, although it applied the correction in all 20 of its own. We report the effect of two problems in our shielding items, found after the runs, and release the code, per-item outcomes and targeted-test responses.

##### 2611.05341v1 2026-11-03T18:41:15Z
Weight-space programming for auditing clinical decision networks
AUTHORS: Humza Nusrat, Omar Nusrat
Machine learning models in radiotherapy are commissioned by testing them on cases with known answers, which may not reveal a shortcut that the test cases share with the training data. Frontier language models have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of small neural networks, an ability called weight-space programming. The purpose of this study was to determine whether such a model, given only a clinical protocol and a network's weights, can audit and repair the network. Networks with 433 to 4,801 parameters were trained to screen head-and-neck planning requests against four rules. Flaws were planted through the training data: confounds that hid each rule, a 3 Gy shift in the cord threshold, and a hidden trigger. Claude Opus 5.5 audited each network blind, without tools, data or code execution, and every claim and repair was tested on about 420,000 requests. The language model named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks (95% CI 67% to 97%), including all 15 with a confound or a threshold shift. # Silicon Valley‘s political spending spree meets a blue wave — and a data center revolt

Tech billionaires poured hundreds of millions into the midterms, but it didn’t buy them much.

Published Nov. 4, 2026 at 12:25 a.m.

Tuesday’s election results were a repudiation of the Trump administration, but also of another power center across the country: Silicon Valley.
Tech billionaires like Elon Musk and venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz poured historic amounts of money into this year’s midterms, only to see their chosen candidates bulldozed by a blue wave. And AI safety candidates and critics of data center construction saw major wins, despite millions of dollars in spending from industry PACs.
By Tuesday night, Democratic advisers were declaring victory — and delivering a warning to Big Tech.

ADVERTISEMENT

“The biggest names in tech decided two years ago to stand behind a president who had sold out and screwed over every person he has ever done business with and thought they would get the better of him,” said Cooper Teboe, a Silicon Valley donor adviser and chief strategist to Rep. Ro Khanna. “They lost out, made terrible political investments across the country, and I suspect will spend the next two years paying the price.”
Musk was the biggest loser of the night. The richest man in the world poured nearly half a billion dollars into efforts to elect Republicans across the country — including nearly $216 million to his self-funded America PAC — but Democrats still won control of the House and Senate, as well as key gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. An especially painful race was the Texas Senate contest, where Republican Ken Paxton lost to Democrat James Talarico — whom Musk had spent more than $200 million trying to defeat.

More about AI Is Eating SF

# Would you hate data centers less if they were called ‘AI compute campuses’?

-

# Why Gavin Newsom faces a ‘no-win situation’ with billionaire tax

-

# Can mathematicians count on AI? A Stanford professor weighs in

Voters also handed a stinging rebuke to the AI and crypto industries, and to billionaires like Andreessen and Horowitz who funded their political operations. Sherrod Brown, whom the crypto industry helped oust from Congress in 2024, won his Ohio Senate race Tuesday, despite $55 million in spending against him from cryptocurrency PACs. Brown made fighting the rising energy costs associated with AI data centers central to his populist campaign and promised to “stand up to Big Tech” if elected.
Indeed, despite debate about whether issues related to data centers and AI were important to voters this cycle, they appeared to be surprisingly relevant in exit polling. An NBC poll (opens in new tab) Tuesday night found that 56% of voters said AI or data centers were a “crucial or major factor” in their congressional vote. And as of that evening, it appeared that at least 35 local ballot measures banning or limiting data center construction across the country were set to pass.
In another shocking loss for the AI industry, Darline Graham — who replaced her brother Lindsey Graham in Congress after his death — lost her bid for Senate in South Carolina to Democrat Annie Andrews. Graham had drawn millions from pro-AI PACs, including American Mission and Building the Future. Andrews capitalized on the donations, dubbing Graham “Data Center Darline,” and called for a two-year moratorium on data center construction in the state.
Meanwhile, a number of AI regulation proponents won close congressional races. In Colorado, Manny Rutinel, the sponsor of early state legislation targeting AI companies, ousted the Republican incumbent; in Kansas, regulatory proponent and Democrat Adam Hamilton did the same. Rutinel, in particular, was a favorite of donors working in and around frontier AI labs who are concerned about the risks of the technology — a burgeoning group who contributed millions of dollars to pro-regulation candidates this cycle.
Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff spoke to AI safety concerns in his victory speech Tuesday night, specifically calling out the “titans of Silicon Valley [who] dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”
And Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, was already calling on Democrats to make AI a top priority going forward, saying in a statement that Congress should “investigate how these companies are putting the jobs, freedom, and lives of Americans at risk.”
In one twist, Republican Byron Donalds — who has repeatedly expressed support for building data centers in the U.S. — won his race for Florida governor, riding on millions in contributions from pro-AI PAC Leading the Future and developers of data centers. And in Florida’s 25th District, the Leading the Future-backed Democrat Jared Moskowitz defeated Republican Scott Singer, who was supported by pro-regulation PAC Public First Action.
Silicon Valley also seemed poised for victory closer to home in California, where a coalition of tech titans came together to fight Prop 40 — an effort to levy 5% tax on the wealth of the state’s billionaires. Prominent figures including Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison donated more than $340 million to oppose the measure, which was trailing in the polls Tuesday night.
Still, opponents of the AI industry seemed to be reading the election results as a clear-cut victory. On Tuesday night, Shaunna Thomas — director of the Guardrails Alliance, a PAC that fights AI money in politics — posted on X (opens in new tab) that Democratic leaders should “absorb this remarkably clear lesson: Aligning with Big Tech is a political catastrophe.”

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez urged the agency not to allow AI-generated robocalls in the lead-up to the midterms, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer also opposed the request, per MS NOW. I found no result confirming whether the FCC acted on it.
- **Background:** The 2024 New Hampshire robocall used an AI voice resembling Biden. Days after that, the FCC banned the use of AI-generated voices in robocalls. The FCC's current position on the Club for Growth petition is the open question.
- **Deepfake ads:** One report says 69% of the AI campaign ads that surfaced this midterm season were missing AI disclaimers. The FEC remains stalled on comprehensive AI advertising rules, and Texas prohibits publishing a deepfake video intended to influence voters within 30 days of an election.
- **Chatbots:** A Washington Post review found top AI chatbots getting basic information wrong at rates as high as 48 percent across AI-generated voter guides. A Pew survey found just eight percent of US voters say they've used an AI chatbot to look up ballot information.
- **Base-rate context:** After 2024, Al Jazeera reported that the anticipated avalanche of AI-driven misinformation never materialised, and that viral misinformation was mostly "cheap fakes," authentic content deceptively edited without AI.

For election-day incidents or the FCC's final decision, a follow-up search for the FCC ruling or post-election AI incident reports would be needed.

The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token’s residual stream encodes the label’s identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query’s class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. Georgia 2026 Election Results: Winners in Key Races - Capital B News - Atlanta

Supporters hold up signs and cheer as they wait for former President Barack Obama to speak at a midterm campaign rally Wednesday in Morrow, Georgia. Obama joined U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff and Democrat gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms at the rally. (Photo by Erik S. Lesser/AFP via Getty Images)

Black Georgians accounted for roughly 30% of early votes cast ahead of today’s Nov. 3 election, helping drive record midterm turnout across the state.

Below are the Georgia 2026 election results for key state and local races. This page will be updated as winners are announced.

STATE RACES

# Governor

Winner: Keisha Lance Bottoms

Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms faced a bruising campaign against billionaire healthcare CEO Rick Jackson.

Bottoms, vying to be the first Black woman to serve as governor in the U.S., campaigned on a plan to expand Medicaid, fund pre-K, restore reproductive rights, and pause construction on data centers. She also called out Jackson’s allegiance to President Donald Trump.

Jackson, a political novice who touted a promise to be Trump’s favorite president, focused on crime rates in a searing spate of attack ads. He also campaigned on improving affordability, support for Georgia’s agriculture industry, tackling the state’s healthcare and education.

# U.S. Senate

Winner: Sen. Jon Ossoff

Incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff faced off against scandal-plagued Republican Mike Collins and secured an early victory tonight securing 64.5% of the vote. AP called the race around 8:00 p.m.

A major component of Ossoff’s campaign platform centered on tackling Georgia’s affordability and housing challenges . Ossoff, who received 92% of Georgia’s Black vote in 2021, polled ahead of Collins for most of the race, calling Collins a “bigot” who is unfit for office.

While he has repeatedly rebuffed calls, Ossoff is considered one of the frontrunners for a 2028 White House run.

# Attorney General

Winner: Tanya Miller

Facing off against Republican state Sen. Brian Strickland, Tanya Miller campaigned on reining in grocery store supply chains and utility companies as she focused on the state’s affordability crisis. The civil rights attorney and Democratic state House representative from Atlanta also said she would sue to block some of the Trump administration’s federal government cuts from taking full effect.

Strickland is the self-described conservative lawmaker who centered his campaign on going after violent criminals, including gangs, drug dealers and human traffickers.

# Secretary of State

Winner: Penny Brown Reynolds

Penny Brown Reynolds , a former Fulton County judge and star of Family Court with Judge Penny , ran on protecting voting rights against Trump-endorsed Republican Rep. Tim Fleming. The U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais nullified a key portion of the 1965 Voting Rights Act.

Brown Reynolds launched her bid last year in response to Republican-led efforts to scrutinize voter access in Georgia. That includes the 2021 enactment of SB 202 , the law that reduced absentee ballot drop box access in largely Black Fulton County and allowed tens of thousands of Georgians to have their voter eligibility challenged .

Fleming, a Republican state lawmaker and small-business owner from Covington, made preserving “election integrity” a central focus in his own secretary of state bid.

# Public Service Commission

Winners: Peter Hubbard and Sheila Edwards

Democrats gained control of the Public Service Commission for the first time in more than 20 years.

##### 2611.05345v1 2026-11-03T18:45:23Z
Hongyin Luo, Wei Fang, Lijie Yang, Owen Stepan, Daniel Suit, Jeff Krapf, Dana Wensberg, Jack O'Brien
Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

##### 2611.05272v1 2026-11-03T17:55:57Z
Adar Peleg, Dvir Alsheich, Tomer Ashuach, Avi Mendelson
Evaluating whether a large language model (LLM) genuinely knows a concept remains a fundamental problem, since behavioral metrics can be fooled by suppression: a model that refuses to answer may still harbor recoverable knowledge. The framework measures the geometric coherence of \textit{anon-vectors}, the differences in hidden states between a concept-specific query and its anonymized paraphrase, and shows that genuine knowledge forms a tight, low-entropy cluster while ignorance forces geometric fragmentation. Across ten instruction-tuned LLMs from three model families, all fragmentation metrics reliably separate known from unknown concepts, and post-unlearning, fragmentation geometry correlates with adversarial recovery across four attack types and five unlearning algorithms, though the direction of that relationship is shown to depend on attack methodology. Furthermore, a layer-resolved analysis reveals that different adversarial mechanisms exploit this geometry at varying depths, with high attack-specific correlations that are invisible to behavioral evaluation. Together, these results constitute a single-phase, attack-free proxy for unlearning robustness that captures aspects of parametric knowledge inaccessible to output-level metrics. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/AdarPeleg/geometry-of-ignorance

##### 2611.05108v1 2026-11-03T16:02:34Z
Jeremy Qin, Ruizhi Deng, Mohamed Osama Ahmed, Frederick Tung, Leo Feng
Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.

Americans Reject Use of AI for Medical and Coverage Decisions

- Article

- 0 Comments

Most Americans don’t want artificial intelligence making decisions about their medical care and insurance, according to a new Pew Research Center report.

While Americans are generally open to AI use in healthcare for tasks like translating, 60% of the 3,488 US adults Pew surveyed in June said they were uncomfortable with AI helping their doctor make a diagnosis or treatment plans.

Anthropic, OpenAI and other tech giants herald AI as a way to make improvements to healthcare and have encouraged its widespread adoption. Yet nearly half of Americans believe AI will worsen their patient-doctor relationship and are split on whether it will improve patient outcomes.

“They generally don’t want AI operating solo,” Eileen Yam, the director of science and society research at Pew Research Center and lead author of the report, said in an interview. “They want a human in the loop doing final reviews.”

Only 5% of Americans were open to insurance claim decisions being made by AI without human review, and almost half of respondents said they did not want AI to play any role these decisions, according to the report.

Patients say they trust doctors to use AI in their best interests over health insurance companies, federal or state-level government, tech firms or hospital leadership.

More than half of respondents also said that they see AI posing a risk to their personal health information.

Americans’ attitudes were similar to what Pew Research found in 2022 , but there was a broader negative shift among younger adults around AI in general.

As tech companies continue to promote AI in healthcare as a priority, Yam said that transparency will be key.

“For ordinary Americans navigating a world where AI is increasingly part of healthcare, we see in our data that their views on AI in healthcare are not a binary ‘thumbs up’ versus ‘thumbs down,'” she said. “Americans just want to be informed when AI is being used in their care.”

Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session.

Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks.

Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms.

results:
The search turned up coverage of a Hy4 release, but the sources disagree on timing and the benchmark numbers are mostly Tencent's own.

**Timing conflict:** Several sources describe a "Hy4 preview" released on August 28, 2026. One says a 770B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 49B active per token, a 1M-token context, and an Apache 2.0 license. A separate FourWeekMBA article says Tencent released Hy4 on 4 November at $0.834 per million input tokens and $2.501 per million output tokens, and that it is based on a Tencent release page dated 4 November 2026. I could not confirm which is the full release and which is the preview, so treat the November date as a single-source claim.

**Benchmarks (all vendor-reported or unverified):**
- Tencent's internal blind evaluation put Hy4 preview at 2.99/4.00, versus 2.94 for Kimi K3 and 2.92 for GLM-5.3. One review calls this a near-tie, and says its own chart shows it trading wins and losses with those rivals.
- Reported public scores include 92.3 on GPQA Diamond and 82.9 on SWE-bench Multilingual.
- In Tencent's table for the November release, Hy4 scores 75.2 on APEX-Agents v1.1, compared with 74.8 for Claude Opus 5.5. The FourWeekMBA author notes they ran no tests and have not verified any score independently.
- On the Arena leaderboard, one account reported Hy4 preview placing around #5 in Code Arena's WebDev category, though it was an early placement from automated voting, not a settled rank.

**Open-source status:** Hugging Face FlagOS repackages derive their weights from the Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy4-preview release and say they are open‑sourced under the Apache License 2.0.

- **Published:** Wednesday 4 November 2026 at 10:09am, updated at 1:28pm (time zone not stated).
- **Jobs affected:** About 1,270. The article says these roles are affected by job cuts, changed roles, or relocation, so not all will be eliminated.

Pinal translates diverse functional prompts into high-quality protein candidates. Credit: Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11205-z

In a short space of time, artificial intelligence has become a whiz at designing proteins, molecular machines that perform various functions such as speeding up reactions, producing fluorescent signals and breaking down plastic. But getting AI to design the specific protein you want usually requires the user to have a strong understanding of molecular structures and geometric constraints to guide the models correctly.

Well, that requirement may soon be a thing of the past.

Scientists led by a team at Westlake University in China have developed a large-scale AI model called Pinal that can generate candidate proteins from natural language prompts alone. They detail their research and how their AI model works in a paper published in the journal Nature .

# Turning words into protein designs

All a user has to do is enter a written description of the job they want the protein to do. For example, they might type something like "design a fluorescent protein that emits green light under illumination."

Pinal, which uses two main modules, takes this description and builds a 1D structural blueprint using its first module, T2struct. A second module, SaProt-T, reads that blueprint and uses the original text prompt to generate a matching amino acid sequence. "Pinal translates high-level functional descriptions into candidate protein sequences, thereby reducing reliance on manually specified structural templates or geometric constraints," wrote the study authors.

One of the many clever things about Pinal is that it doesn't just pick the first shape that comes along. It creates several structural blueprints, designs the best sequence for each and scores each pair to determine the best final design.

Training Pinal required vast amounts of data. The team started with 135 million protein sequences and used AI models and existing protein annotations to build plain-language descriptions of what those proteins do. This resulted in a massive library of 1.7 billion protein-text pairs. They then obtained the predicted 3D structures for those sequences from an existing AlphaFold database .

To test Pinal, the researchers asked it to design four different proteins. These were a fluorescent protein, a plastic-breaking enzyme, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein.

So how well did it do?

# Mixed results

For the glowing protein, it created 50,000 sequences. These were filtered down to 29 for testing, and only one actually fluoresced. The researchers acknowledged that controlling specific properties is still difficult. "For example, prompting for a precise emission wavelength in a fluorescent protein remains challenging."

The system was better at producing the metabolic H-protein shuttle. Five of the 20 candidates worked, and the best one boosted the output of a key carbon-capturing process to 1.7 times that achieved using the natural E. coli protein.

While much of this is promising, Pinal still has limitations. Further work is needed before it becomes a routine lab tool.

# Abstract
Spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity while preserving the locations of cells within tissue. A key analysis step is to divide the tissue into spatial domains, but the performance of computational methods varies considerably across datasets, and no single method consistently performs best. Here we show that a large language model can compare spatial domain maps and identify the better-performing methods. We developed L-STAR, which visually compares and ranks candidate methods, then builds a consensus map from the highest-ranked results. Across datasets representing different tissues, species, and technologies, L-STAR matched expert annotations more closely than individual methods or consensus analysis using a fixed set of methods. Its rankings were reproducible and generally stable when image colors or presentation order changed. L-STAR also provided rationales for its comparisons and assigned biologically meaningful names to the detected domains. These findings show that large language models can make spatial transcriptomics analysis more adaptive, robust, and interpretable.

# Abstract
Accurate particle picking of macromolecules of diverse types, shapes and sizes in cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is critical for understanding the molecular architecture of biological systems in their native state. Current deep learning methods have shown potential for identifying macromolecules in tomograms; however, they are vulnerable to annotation noise in the training data and to imbalanced distributions of macromolecule species. Here, to address these limitations, we developed RobPicker, a meta-learning framework that effectively mitigates these issues by automatically learning to correct label errors and by placing greater emphasis on smaller and rarer macromolecule species. In evaluations across diverse cryo-ET datasets with noisy labels and imbalanced species distributions, RobPicker substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in identifying small and rare macromolecules. The robustness and efficiency of RobPicker led to improved resolution in 3D density maps of protein structures, enabling high-resolution cellular structural biology analysis.

results:
The PATIENT AI Act is a discussion draft from Senate HELP Chairman Bill Cassidy, released October 29, 2026. It has not been introduced or voted on, and comments are due December 1.

- **FDA and ONC roles:** The draft would settle which AI tools fall under FDA oversight and which fall under ONC. Tools that don't qualify as FDA-regulated devices would fall under ONC's certified health IT program.
- **FDA changes:** The draft would give the FDA a risk-based review process for software devices, including authority to accept premarket software changes so updated tools reach patients faster. It would also let the agency review software changes on a rolling basis.
- **Payment:** The draft would create a Medicare payment pathway. One report says it would direct Medicare to test paying for autonomous clinical AI while requiring patient notice and preserving appeal rights.
- **Open questions:** Who is liability when autonomous AI causes harm remains an open question that the draft sends to further study through a nonprofit review.
- **Context:** Cassidy's office describes the aim as a more predictable and consistent framework to review and reimburse for AI-based technologies. One outlet notes the draft also restates federal preemption of state product liability laws for these devices.

Coverage is consistent across outlets. The main caveat is that all of this comes from early reporting on a draft, so specific provisions could change before any bill is introduced.

**What was measured:**

- **Hardware:** An MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, an RTX Spark laptop with up to 128GB of unified memory. The DGX Spark desktop served as a comparison point.
- **Firmware:** The Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework, a Windows-visible component that manages power sharing between CPU and GPU. The article says the firmware's power table is encrypted, and only Windows can decrypt it.

  - Power source: on battery, Linux reached about 61 to 67 tokens/s in LM Studio. Plugged in, it dropped to about 15 tokens/s, with clocks falling from about 1,800 MHz to about 780 MHz.
  - Controller test: disabling the controller on Windows dropped throughput from about 83 to 31 tokens/s and clocks from about 2 GHz to 786 MHz.

response.stdout:
License: CC BY 4.0

arXiv:2611.05287v1 [cs.CL] 03 Nov 2026

# Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment

Ariana M. Villegas-Suarez*

Affiliation: LASR Labs

  
Guido Freire*

Affiliation: LASR Labs

  
Sohan Venkatesh*

Affiliation: LASR Labs

  
Bartosz Cywiński

Affiliation: Warsaw University of Technology

# Abstract

Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment.
Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency.
We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes.
When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment.
These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.

Binance says the hackers behind last week’s $6.34 billion theft reached its wallet signing systems after a months-long campaign that compromised three engineers’ computers, one of them through a fake job interview.

The exchange published its initial incident report on November 3. Roughly $2.85 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted.

“This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance said.

The FBI has blamed the theft on TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group.

# How the attack unfolded

According to Binance, the intrusion unfolded in stages and relied on fake recruiters, malicious downloads, hijacked employee computers and an internal AI tool. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company noted.

The campaign started in June, when a Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while looking for a popular AI coding tool through a search engine. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Binance’s security team caught it, swapped out his device and reset the related credentials. Even so, the attackers had already gained insight into what he did and who he worked with on the wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a second engineer was approached by someone claiming to be a project director. He was invited to two interviews, the first with a fake HR representative and the second with the alleged CEO of a company that did not exist.

During the first interview, the HR impostor shared a social media account containing personal photos and videos to build rapport. The second took place over a chat app and ended with a request to download a coding “assignment” onto his work computer.

The assignment hid a malicious code repository that executed as soon as the engineer set it up. The malware substituted a rogue copy of a legitimate developer tool component and opened a channel to a server run by the attackers.

“The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time,” Binance said.

On October 20, the attackers used the infected machine and an internal AI tool to gain control of the first engineer’s system and a third wallet engineer’s system. The report does not explain how the AI tool was used.

The first engineer’s computer held a token that allowed container deployments. On October 29, the attackers signed into the third engineer’s computer, deployed a container with credentials taken from the first engineer and kicked off the attack with a malicious script.

Binance says the attackers exploited unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to move XRP, SOL, OP and BTC out of its hot wallets. The same service was used to abuse Ethereum’s EIP-7702 mechanism, giving a contract under the attackers’ control partial execution rights over a hot wallet.

“However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure,” the company explained.

The hot wallet was secured with multi-party computation (MPC), which meant Binance had no single key it could use to cancel the delegation right away. The last unauthorized transfer settled at 23:56 UTC, and the delegation was cleared shortly after midnight.

Binance says it has rebuilt the affected wallet system and AI tool, replaced devices and retired the engineers’ credentials and tokens. It is engaging independent security firms to review the incident and is working on a research fund focused on AI security in blockchain environments.

The exchange also disclosed that it had detected and blocked 57 suspected North Korea-linked threats this year.

# Other developments

North Korea has rejected the FBI’s attribution of the heist to its TraderTraitor hackers. “It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds,” Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement carried by state media.

[ Read : North Korea Launches Missiles Toward the Sea to Protest Binance Hack Claims ]

Binance has also completed a zero-knowledge proof for its October 31 reserves snapshot, which lets holders of 10 major tokens verify that their balances are backed at least 1:1. Co-CEO Richard Teng says 98% of the impacted tokens have now been replenished .

Teng also said on November 3 that withdrawals have broadly resumed. The exchange began reopening them in phases on November 1.

On the laundering front, Elliptic says the stolen funds passed through about 12,000 wallets on 11 blockchains in under four days, using automation but with no sign of AI agents making decisions. As of November 3, roughly $3.18 billion remained in theft-linked addresses. Separately, Chainalysis said an emergency pause at THORChain, triggered by an unrelated technical issue, had temporarily slowed the laundering .

Dreadnode, founded in 2023, develops offensive AI security tools. The startup raised $14 million in Series A funding in early 2025.

According to CrowdStrike, Dreadnode’s platform lets users describe in plain language what they want to test. It then runs more than 100 known AI attack strategies, including jailbreaks, prompt injection, and multi-turn and agent-specific attacks.

The tests target AI models, agent reasoning loops, applications and MCP servers. Findings are ranked by severity, mapped to frameworks such as the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, MITRE ATLAS and the NIST AI RMF, and fed to CrowdStrike’s Falcon Guardian AI detection and response product as policy recommendations.

The Dreadnode team, led by CEO Brad Palm, will join CrowdStrike’s Cyber Superintelligence Lab. Dreadnode-based testing capabilities are expected to become generally available in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

Alongside the acquisitions, CrowdStrike introduced an AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian that allows authorized administrators to halt a misbehaving AI agent, prevent it from restarting, and cut off its network access.

CrowdStrike has made several security acquisitions over the past year. In January, it announced plans to buy identity security firm SGNL for $740 million and browser security company Seraphic for a reported $420 million. In September 2025, it agreed to acquire AI security firm Pangea .

- Virtual Events

# ICS:

Meta has paid roughly $1.2 million in bug bounties for its Muse AI agent, including $300,000 for a pre-launch flaw that exposed data on internal test systems.

Muse is a personal AI agent that acts on a user’s behalf across their email, calendar, messaging and other accounts. Each user’s agent gets its own virtual machine.

The bug bounty program ran privately from April and went public at the agent’s September 8 launch, Meta’s David Singleton said in a blog post . Of the more than 630 reports received, 64 were valid.

The $300,000 reward was handed out four months before launch, while Muse was at an early internal testing stage. The researcher demonstrated access to conversations and tokens on pre-release VMs used by Meta staff to test the product.

“An authentication check treated a header added by a local HTTPS proxy as proof that a request came from a trusted source. During a system migration, the environment gained a second proxy layer. That meant requests from outside could carry the trusted header too,” Singleton explained.

Meta took the service offline, fixed the bug and stopped treating the local machine as trusted. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

A $90,000 bounty was paid for a report involving a malicious web page that, when Muse was asked to summarize it, mimicked status messages from the agent’s browsing tool. “It got the agent to execute some actions which should have been caught,” Singleton noted.

Meta has since added detection signals and changed how Muse treats tool output that looks suspicious. It says that, in testing, its classifiers now catch the attack and 100 variants.

Another $90,000 went to a report showing that specific formatting could slip one-time passcodes past Muse’s email redaction filters. Meta described it as one piece of an end-to-end attack.

A $50,000 reward went to an Android app flaw that let a malicious app pass a link to a privileged web view. “The link handler recognized a shared-page path without validating its host and loaded it,” Singleton wrote, allowing an attacker’s page to grab the web view’s credentials.

A $1,000 bounty covered a Mac app flaw that let an attacker with access to the computer hijack the auto-update feature to execute code with the app’s permissions.

Meta pays up to $300,000 per valid report, which it claims is several times more than the top rewards advertised by other leading AI developers. Prompt injection attacks affecting a single user can earn up to $130,000, while a fleetwide compromise can earn as much as $250,000.
